items.titleOriginal: Suitcase-sized robot learns to flow with crowds instead of freezing up

items.descriptionOriginal: Robots that treat every person as an obstacle tend to freeze in dense crowds. Researchers at Örebro University in Sweden have developed a navigation system that teaches robots the “unwritten rules” of human movement, helping them keep moving through crowds. In the long term, the technology could serve as a digital complement to guide dogs for people with visual impairments. The work was published in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). Why robots freeze Navigating a busy train station or airport is a major challenge for people with visual impairments. Today’s navigation robots do not make it easier, because they treat each person as an obstacle to avoid. When a crowd gets too dense, such robots can suffer from what researchers call the “freezing robot problem” and stop completely because no clear path is available. People behave differently. We do not stop in a crowd; we adapt, keep to one side and move with the flow, and the Örebro team built its approach on that observation. Maps of dynamics Yufei Zhu, who recently defended his doctoral thesis in computer science, developed what are known as “Maps of Dynamics.” Rather than mapping only fixed features such as walls and doorways, the robot learns how people typically move through a particular place at different times of day. Zhu compares it to a newcomer arriving in a town, observing how locals behave and copying them. By studying movement flows, the robot learns the patterns and can predict where people are heading. The technology, called HiCrowd, means the robot no longer sees a crowd as a threat or an obstacle. Instead, it uses people’s movement patterns as guidance. Tested at Expo 2025 The system was tested in real-world settings at the Science Museum Miraikan in Tokyo and at Expo 2025 in Osaka. The robot, which resembles a small suitcase, had to make its way through dense streams of visitors. In one test, the robot crossed a crowded hall behind a group of people. When the group turned right, the robot followed even though it could not yet see why. A few seconds later, the reason became clear: a large crowd was walking directly toward them. By following the people ahead, the robot safely passed the oncoming flow without stopping once. Tests also showed that people nearby neither appeared alarmed by the robot nor kept their distance. It blended so naturally into the flow that people treated it like any other pedestrian. A digital guide dog Such a robot, Zhu said, “has to move naturally and follow the flow.” A robot guiding someone through a busy terminal must move smoothly, without abrupt movements or constant stopping, Zhu said. At stations, clear habits and movement patterns mean a guide robot could help a visually impaired person move with the flow, not against it, Zhu said. Guide dogs are scarce; earlier reporting noted China has just over 400 for almost 20 million blind people, one reason robotic alternatives are being explored. The research was carried out at Örebro University under Professor Martin Magnusson, in close collaboration with the Miraikan Accessibility Lab in Tokyo and Bosch in Germany. The dynamic mapping technology has been applied in settings ranging from warehouse robots in industrial environments to service robots among large groups of museum visitors.

items.descriptionOriginal: Στους μουσικούς δρόμους της Βραζιλίας, της Βενεζουέλας και της Αργεντινής θα ταξιδέψει το κοινό μέσα από τη συναυλία μουσικής δωματίου που διοργανώνει η Αντιδημαρχία Πολιτισμού και Τουρισμού του Δήμου Πυλαίας – Χορτιάτη, τη Δευτέρα 30 Νοεμβρίου 2026, στις 20:00, στο Αμφιθέατρο «Σταύρος Κουγιουμτζής» του Δημαρχείου Πανοράματος. Η είσοδος για το κοινό είναι ελεύθερη. Τέσσερις καταξιωμένοι μουσικοί, η Χριστίνα Λαζαρίδου και ο Μιγκέλ Μιχαηλίδης στο βιολί, η Ρόζα Τερζιάν στη βιόλα και ο Ιωάννης Στέφος στο βιολοντσέλο, θα παρουσιάσουν τρία εμβληματικά έργα του 20ού αιώνα για κουαρτέτο εγχόρδων. Με αφορμή τη συναυλία, ο δήμαρχος Πυλαίας – Χορτιάτη και πρόεδρος της ΠΕΔΚΜ, Ιγνάτιος Καϊτεζίδης, δήλωσε: « Στον δήμο μας επενδύουμε σταθερά στον ποιοτικό πολιτισμό, καθώς ο πολιτισμός και οι τέχνες είναι κομμάτια της καθημερινότητας και της ποιότητας ζωής που θέλουμε για τους συμπολίτες μας. Φέρνουμε στο Πανόραμα τέσσερις εξαιρετικούς μουσικούς και ένα ρεπερτόριο που σπάνια έχουμε την ευκαιρία να απολαύσουμε ζωντανά, με ελεύθερη είσοδο για όλους. Καλώ τους δημότες μας, και ιδιαίτερα τη νέα γενιά, να γεμίσουν το Αμφιθέατρο “Σταύρος Κουγιουμτζής” ». Από την πλευρά της, η αντιδήμαρχος Πολιτισμού και Τουρισμού, Βίκυ Κανέλλου, σημείωσε: « Η μουσική δωματίου έχει μια μοναδική αμεσότητα. Σου επιτρέπει να παρακολουθείς από κοντά τον διάλογο ανάμεσα στα τέσσερα όργανα και τον τρόπο που μια μελωδία περνά από το ένα στο άλλο. Στη συναυλία αυτή, το ίδιο κουαρτέτο θα μας συστήσει τρεις διαφορετικούς συνθέτες, προσφέροντας μια υπέροχη εμπειρία ακόμα και σε όσους θα ακούσουν μουσική δωματίου για πρώτη φορά ». www.ertnews.gr

items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers at Rice University in Houston have made synthetic graphite in just 0.2 seconds using a single electrical pulse. In laboratory tests, the material handled a charging rate equivalent to a four-minute charge, pointing to a way to speed up lithium-ion batteries. The study used petroleum coke, a low-cost residue from oil refining, as the starting material. By adding a nickel compound before applying the pulse, the team produced an anode material that could improve charging while reducing the energy needed to make synthetic graphite. Turning refinery residue into graphite The researchers mixed a small amount of a nickel compound into the petroleum coke. A single electrical pulse briefly heated the mixture to about 4,532°F, allowing the carbon atoms to arrange themselves around tiny nickel particles. The resulting graphite had tightly ordered layers and few defects. “The nickel acts almost like a temporary construction worker, helping the carbon atoms organize themselves into a highly ordered, layered graphite structure,” said Haojie Zhu, a Rice University postdoctoral associate and the study’s first author. “Usually, creating graphite requires prolonged heating at extremely high temperatures for long periods, but this method allows us to do it in just two-tenths of a second,” he added. Temperature mattered. When the mixture got too hot, much of the nickel was lost. At lower temperatures, the graphite formed with a less ordered structure. The capacity of retention During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite anode and settle between its layers. How quickly those ions can enter and move through the graphite helps determine how fast a lithium-ion battery can charge. The nickel-assisted process slightly widened the gaps between those layers, making it easier for lithium ions to enter. In a laboratory battery, the new material outperformed conventional graphite during fast charging. The battery also retained 80% of its capacity after 1,000 full charge and discharge cycles. The improved performance persisted after the researchers removed more than 99% of the residual nickel. That result suggests the nickel’s main role was to shape the graphite as it formed, leaving behind a structure that helped lithium ions move through the anode. Using lesser energy The team’s analysis estimated that the method could cut both energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions by more than 80% compared with conventional graphite production. The potential savings come from shortening the high-temperature treatment needed to turn the carbon feedstock into graphite. The process addresses two steps that affect the cost and performance of lithium-ion batteries. Making the anode material requires high temperatures, and once the battery is assembled, the graphite’s structure helps determine how quickly it can take up lithium. The Rice team used the same brief heating step to make the material and widen its layer spacing. “This method could help make future electric vehicle batteries charge faster while reducing the cost and environmental impact of battery manufacturing,” said James Tour , a Rice University chemistry professor and the study’s corresponding author. The study was published in the Advanced Materials journal.

items.descriptionOriginal: A remote zinc mine in northwest Alaska could host the state’s largest solar farm, with more than 15,000 panels spread across about 30 acres. The Alaska Energy Authority (AEA) announced Tuesday that it would lend $4.9 million toward the $35 million project at Red Dog Mine, which relies on diesel shipped to its port near Kivalina. The solar farm would have a peak output of 8.8 megawatts (MW), more than any solar farm currently operating in Alaska. It is expected to be completed in late 2028 and would displace some of the diesel the mine burns to generate electricity. Plans filed with the state put the array’s footprint at about the size of 23 football fields. A small share of a large power bill Red Dog, one of the world’s largest zinc mines, typically draws about 25 MW of power, roughly seven times the city of Kotzebue’s peak demand. Its eight diesel generators burn about 40,000 gallons of fuel a day, or nearly 15 million gallons a year, according to previously published figures from Teck. The company’s Alaska subsidiary, which operates the mine, expects to spend $40 million to $45 million on energy this year. AEA Executive Director Curtis Thayer estimates the solar farm would supply about 5% of the mine’s current power needs. The 8.8-MW figure represents the array’s maximum output. The amount of electricity it can supply over time depends on how much sunlight reaches the panels. “It’s nice to have renewables supporting a mining activity. It’s a balance,” Thayer said. “The one thing is it displaces diesel, and diesel is very expensive.” Solar power for cleanup after closure Red Dog is expected to close in 2031 unless Teck develops nearby deposits. Closing the mine would sharply reduce electricity demand. Once mining stops, Thayer estimates the solar farm could meet about 90% of the site’s remaining power needs, most of which would come from cleanup work. “There’s remediation that has to be done once the mine is closed, and so this will pay for that,” Thayer said. A state loan for a privately operated array The loan will go to Tugliq RedDog1, a subsidiary of Canadian energy company Tugliq. The subsidiary will build, own and operate the solar farm and sell the electricity to Teck. Thayer said the loan carries a 5.5% interest rate, compared with a market rate of about 6.6%. He said he believes this is the first time the AEA’s Power Project Fund has lent money to support a mine. The agency offers below-market financing to help make energy more affordable and reliable in Alaska. Thayer said the AEA expects the loan to be repaid even if Red Dog closes on schedule. Teck has been looking at renewable power for Red Dog for several years. It installed a weather tower in 2024 to assess the site’s potential for wind power and first proposed the solar farm in March. The original proposal called for construction to begin by June to qualify for federal tax credits that were set to expire in July.

items.descriptionOriginal: A borewell can run dry without much warning. For a farmer depending on it to irrigate crops or a family relying on it for everyday water needs, the question that follows is simple: how much water is actually left underground? Finding an answer is not easy. Unlike rivers, lakes, or reservoirs, groundwater reserves cannot be seen. Their availability depends on several factors, from rainfall and soil conditions to the rate at which water is extracted. Without reliable estimates, planning how much to draw or where to focus conservation efforts becomes difficult. By analysing historical borewell records, rainfall patterns and soil characteristics, JALAAKAR attempts to make underground water reserves easier to understand. Photograph: ( Firstpost ) A school student from Surat, Gujarat, is exploring how technology could make this information easier to access. Dheyay Shah has developed JALAAKAR, a machine-learning-based tool that estimates groundwater availability across different talukas using historical records and environmental data. His innovation recently won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026, a nationwide challenge that received more than 6,100 project submissions from school students across India. Making groundwater easier to understand India depends heavily on groundwater for drinking water, agriculture and other everyday needs. However, excessive extraction, changing rainfall patterns and growing demand have put pressure on these underground reserves. One of the difficulties in managing this resource is knowing how much water is available in a particular area. Groundwater levels can vary depending on local geography, the amount of rainfall received, and how much water is being extracted. This is where Dheyay's project comes in. Instead of relying on isolated measurements, JALAAKAR brings together different sources of information to generate estimates that help people better understand groundwater conditions. How JALAAKAR uses machine learning At its core, JALAAKAR uses machine learning to identify patterns in historical groundwater and environmental data. The tool considers information such as past borewell records, rainfall patterns, and soil characteristics. Each of these offers a different piece of information about underground water reserves. For instance, rainfall influences how much water can seep into the ground and replenish aquifers. Soil characteristics determine how readily this water can percolate, while borewell records provide insights into changes in groundwater levels over time. JALAAKAR analyses these datasets to identify relationships and recurring patterns. It then uses what it learns from the historical information to estimate groundwater availability at the taluka level. JALAAKAR uses historical data to identify patterns and estimate groundwater availability across different talukas. Photograph: ( Digit ) In simpler terms, the tool attempts to use what has happened in the past to understand what groundwater conditions might look like in a particular area. Such estimates could eventually help local communities, farmers, and those involved in water management make more informed decisions about extraction and conservation. However, predictive estimates are not a substitute for actual groundwater measurements. The tool's accuracy, independent field validation, and suitability for different geographical conditions would need to be established before it can be used for wider water-management decisions. A young innovator looking beneath the surface Dheyay's project was recognised at vivo Ignite 2026, where he emerged as the national winner. The competition brought together school students working on ideas that apply science and technology to real-world challenges. With more than 6,100 projects received, the challenge evaluated innovations on parameters such as creativity, scientific application, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and potential social impact. What makes JALAAKAR interesting is the problem it chooses to address. Groundwater management is often discussed in terms of large-scale infrastructure and policy, but it also begins with something much simpler: understanding how much water is available before using it. Dheyay's innovation won the national title at vivo Ignite 2026. Photograph: ( Tehelka ) Dheyay's work explores how data can help answer that question. While the tool would need further testing and refinement before wider application, it offers a promising starting point for making groundwater information more accessible. For a young student, looking beneath the surface has meant looking at a problem that affects millions of people. And if developed further, JALAAKAR could contribute to a future where communities have better information to guide how they use and protect one of their most important natural resources. Sources: 'Dheyay Shah named winner for Vivo Ignite 2026, over 6,100 projects received' by Economic Times, Published on 29 October 2026. 'Surat school student uses machine learning to estimate groundwater availability; project wins national innovation challenge' by Sanjay Sharma for The Times Of India, Published on 10 November 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: What comes to mind when you think of a successful business? Crores in revenue, thousands of employees, a presence across the world, or perhaps a celebrated CEO? Now consider a few other measures of success. How many women earned their first independent income? How many people with disabilities found a workplace where they could build a career? How many families could afford life-saving medical treatment? How many rural artisans could earn a living without leaving their villages? Recent conversations around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's management practices have brought a larger question into focus: what truly makes a good business leader? Closer to home, these five Indian enterprises offer a different perspective on success. From hospitality and healthcare to waste management and handicrafts, they show how building a profitable business can go hand in hand with creating meaningful opportunities and improving people's lives. Making room for every ability At Lemon Tree Hotels, learning Indian Sign Language is part of employee training. It helps colleagues communicate with one another and makes everyday working life more accessible for employees with hearing disabilities. At Lemon Tree Hotels, employees learn Indian Sign Language to build a workplace where everyone can communicate and thrive. Photograph: ( Hotelier India ) Patu Keswani, the founder of the hotel group, began hiring people with disabilities in 2007. Over the years, the company has adapted its training programmes to accommodate people with different needs. Deaf employees receive training with the help of sign language interpreters, while colleagues with low vision are provided accessible learning materials. Some neurodivergent employees undergo internships lasting more than six months to help them settle into their roles. According to its 2025–26 annual report , Lemon Tree employed 305 people with disabilities and another 635 people from socially and economically disadvantaged backgrounds across its owned, leased and managed hotels. Much like several inclusive caf s across India , the hotel chain demonstrates how adapting workplaces to people's needs can open up meaningful career opportunities. Taking village crafts to the world In 1978, Nand Kishore Chaudhary began Jaipur Rugs with two looms and nine artisans. He wanted to connect rural craftspeople directly with larger markets, helping them earn through skills they had developed over generations. Jaipur Rugs connects 40,000 artisans across 600 villages to global markets, creating livelihoods through generations-old weaving skills. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) According to the founder's website , the business has grown to work with around 40,000 artisans across 600 villages in five Indian states. Around 80 percent of them are women. For many of these women, weaving offers an opportunity to earn from their homes without having to migrate to cities or travel far for work. As The Better India previously reported , the company delivers raw materials to artisans' homes and collects the finished carpets from them. Through its Manchaha initiative, artisans also get the freedom to create their own rug designs, drawing inspiration from their surroundings, experiences and imagination. Their craftsmanship has found customers across the world while creating livelihood opportunities closer to home. Making life-saving surgeries affordable For a family struggling to afford heart surgery, the cost of treatment can stand between a loved one and potentially life-saving medical care. It was this challenge that cardiac surgeon Dr Devi Shetty sought to address when he founded Narayana Health in Bengaluru in 2001. Narayana Health's high-volume hospital model helps reduce treatment costs, making specialised cardiac care accessible to more families. Photograph: ( GovInsider ) His hospital model focuses on performing a large number of surgeries, making efficient use of medical equipment and reducing procurement and operational expenses. The savings help bring down the cost of treatment for patients. A 2017 case study by The Commonwealth Fund documented that Narayana Health had brought the average cost of open-heart surgery below US$2,000 at the time. By rethinking how hospitals operate, Dr Shetty built a business model that demonstrates how greater efficiency can help more families access specialised medical care. Helping waste pickers become entrepreneurs When Lotfar moved to Bengaluru in 2010, he was struggling to make ends meet as a waste picker. A 2022 report by Tata Trusts documented how his life changed after he began working with Hasiru Dala. By then, he owned four trucks and employed around 20 other waste pickers. Founded in 2015 by Shekar Prabhakar, Nalini Shekar and Marwan Abubaker, Hasiru Dala Innovations is a waste management enterprise that helps informal waste workers build more secure livelihoods and run their own businesses. Hasiru Dala Innovations helps waste pickers become entrepreneurs, creating businesses around the people who keep cities clean. Photograph: ( Forbes India ) These entrepreneurs provide waste collection and management services to residential communities, offices and events. They earn through service fees as well as the sale of recyclable materials. By 2022, the enterprise had supported 24 waste-picker entrepreneurs, who had, in turn, created employment opportunities for around 300 other waste pickers. The model brings the people who have long helped keep our cities clean into the business of managing their waste, giving them opportunities to grow as entrepreneurs. From making papads to becoming business owners In 1959, seven women in Mumbai borrowed Rs 80 and began making papads. Their aim was simple: to earn an income of their own. What began as a small venture became Shri Mahila Griha Udyog Lijjat Papad, one of India's most recognisable household brands. Lijjat Papad provides self-employment to around 45,000 women, giving them a shared stake in the enterprise. Photograph: (Femina) According to its official website , the enterprise provides self-employment to around 45,000 women across 83 branches in 16 states. What makes Lijjat particularly interesting is its shared ownership model. Its women members participate in running the enterprise, and the profits and losses of each branch are shared among its members. For thousands of women, a skill they already possessed became a means of earning an income and having a stake in the business they helped build. More than six decades later, the enterprise offers an example of what women can achieve when they have access to economic opportunities and collective ownership. These five enterprises have taken different paths to growth. Yet, each offers a valuable lesson in how businesses can widen access to opportunities, recognise overlooked talent and help people build better lives for themselves. Perhaps, alongside asking how much a business earns, we could also ask a question that deserves just as much attention: Who grows when the business grows? items.descriptionOriginal: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Joel Sartore Photo Ark Wildlife Portraits Document 18,567 Species in 25-Year Mission Reading Time: 3 minutes Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits mark two decades of documenting captive species, giving a naked mole rat, a snowy owl, and thousands of others equal time in the spotlight before any could vanish without being seen. Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits began in 2006 at the Lincoln Children’s Zoo near Sartore’s home in Nebraska, with a single photograph of a naked mole rat. Twenty years later, that modest beginning has grown into the largest archive of its kind, totaling 64,436 individual pictures spanning 18,567 species photographed across more than 60 countries. Sartore envisions the project as a 25-year effort to document every species living in human care worldwide. The project’s methodology has remained deliberately consistent over two decades. Joel Sartore’s Photo Ark wildlife portraits are captured against plain black or white backgrounds, stripping away habitat and context so a tiny frog gets the same visual weight and dignity as an elephant or tiger. This approach levels the playing field between charismatic, widely recognized species and overlooked creatures that might otherwise never capture public attention, such as the Palawan stink badger of the Philippines. Sartore does not handle the animals himself during shoots; instead, he relies on zookeepers and animal care staff to safely position each subject. Some aquatic species are photographed through glass enclosures. At the same time, mammals, birds, reptiles, and insects each present their own logistical challenges, from keeping a chimpanzee calm with a caregiver just out of frame to capturing a camera-shy nocturnal porcupine mid-rest. Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits document animals in zoos, aquariums, and wildlife sanctuaries, not creatures photographed in the wild. This focus reflects the project’s core strategy: captive populations often serve as insurance against extinction, and photographing them creates a permanent visual record regardless of what happens to wild populations facing habitat loss, poaching, or climate pressures. The project’s growth trajectory reveals an accelerating pace. Sartore reached 8,000 species roughly a decade into the project, climbed past 11,000 by 2021, surpassed 16,000 by August 2024, and now stands at 18,567, inching toward documenting the full scope of species held in captivity worldwide. Nearly half of all primate species face extinction risk, underscoring the urgency behind photographing vulnerable groups before populations disappear entirely. Portrait of National Geographic photographer and PhotoARK founder Joel Sartore with a frill necked lizard, Chlamydosaurus kingii. Photo by Douglas Gimesy, courtesy of the National Geographic Society . Beyond still photography, Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits have expanded into books including Birds of the Photo Ark and National Geographic Photo Ark Insects, alongside a three-part documentary series titled Rare: Creatures of the Photo Ark. The United States Postal Service further extended the project’s reach by issuing a pane of 20 stamps featuring endangered species drawn directly from Sartore’s portfolio. Public exhibitions have carried the work well beyond magazine pages and museum walls. The Museum of the Shenandoah Valley hosted more than 40 Photo Ark portraits in 2021, and the project’s 20th anniversary brought a dedicated exhibit, Animals of Earth, to the National Geographic Museum of Exploration in Washington, D.C., featuring approximately 17,000 individual wildlife portraits. Among the project’s notable discoveries, Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits have documented entirely new species, including a wild cat native to Bolivia, the first new wild cat species formally described by researchers in over a century, and an undescribed stick insect photographed at the Budapest Zoo. Such discoveries underscore that even as Sartore races to photograph known captive species, new biodiversity continues to emerge from poorly understood corners of the planet. Sartore has been candid about the scale of the task remaining and his own mortality relative to the project’s ambitious scope. He has said a successor will continue the work if he cannot finish, framing the Photo Ark as an effort designed to outlast its founder, with the portraits intended to serve conservation education long after Sartore is gone. The underlying philosophy driving Joel Sartore Photo Ark wildlife portraits centers on a simple but urgent principle: no species should disappear before it has a chance to be documented, however humble or unfamiliar it may seem to the public. Each portrait serves as a scientific record, a conservation advocacy tool , and an artistic statement, insisting that every living creature, regardless of size or popularity, deserves recognition as a living work of art worth saving. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saving Bees From Pesticides and Habitat Loss: Three Steps That Work Reading Time: 3 minutes Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss is possible, and everyday choices make a real difference. Find out how gardens, petitions, and protected land help. Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss is possible, and the plan is already clear. Conservation groups say the work comes down to three actions . First, protect the bee habitat that still exists. Second, add new habitat by planting pollinator-friendly plants in gardens and on public lands. Third, end the worst uses of the pesticides that harm bees. Why does this matter so much? Bees move pollen from flower to flower, helping plants produce fruit and seeds. Around the world, bees pollinate 75% of food crops. That is three out of every four crops. Wild plants lean on bees even more, with 90% of flowering species depending on them. Imagine walking past ten kinds of wildflowers. Nine of them would need bees to reproduce. Losing bees would change both our meals and our landscapes. The problem is growing. As society uses more pesticides, bee populations are plummeting. Pesticides are chemicals made to kill pests, but they can also harm bees. Environment America and its state groups, including Environment Georgia, are pushing for change. One campaign asks Amazon to stop selling bee-killing pesticides. Another asks the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to ban the worst uses of these chemicals. A third petition asks the EPA to pause glyphosate, a common weed killer, until it is proven safe. Each petition gives the public a direct way to push for change. Those voices matter for saving bees and their habitat. Large retailers influence which products reach home gardens. Asking them to drop bee-killing pesticides targets the problem at its source. That makes it easier for everyone to save bees from pesticides and habitat loss. Pesticide concerns reach beyond bees. The group also tracks neonicotinoids, a widely used class of insecticides that kill insects. They have also raised concerns about harm to freshwater species. Habitat is the other half of the story. Bees need safe places to find food and shelter. Protecting the land they already use comes first. Habitat loss means fewer flowers to feed on and fewer places to nest. When bees lose food and homes, whole colonies struggle. That is why saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss must go hand in hand. Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss must go hand in hand, since fewer flowers to feed on and fewer places to nest cause whole colonies to struggle, making protection of the land bees already use the first priority. Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Pexels. Recent updates from the group highlight habitat protection for the rusty patched bumblebee. They also point to roadsides as places where pollinators can thrive. These projects show how saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss can happen close to home. Learning is part of the solution too. The group offers a recorded Save the Bees web-bee-nar, which is an online presentation. Another article explains where bumblebees go in winter and how people can help them. Small efforts build on each other. Each new patch of flowers gives bees another place to feed. Each product you buy instead of one from a shelf lowers the risk they face. Research matters as well. The group urges protection of the U.S. Bee Lab, which works to save bees. Science helps people choose the right steps. Speaking up for saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss takes only a few minutes. The group invites people to add their names to its Amazon and EPA campaigns. Public pressure shows companies and agencies that many people care about bees. Anyone with a garden can add habitat. Pollinator-friendly plants give bees food nearby. Public lands can help too. Some states already have policies to protect pollinators, and the group has published a snapshot of those actions. Gardeners can also think twice before buying bee-killing pesticides. A single garden may seem small. Even a window box or a pot on a front step can serve pollinators. Together, these spaces give bees more places to feed across neighborhoods and cities. Each person has a role in saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss. Homeowners can plant flowers and shoppers can ask stores to change what they sell. Anyone can sign a petition and share what they learn with neighbors. See also: Peru Grants Legal Rights for Stingless Bees in Global First Bees support the food on our plates and the wild plants around us. The tools to protect them already exist. Will you plant a garden, speak up, or do both? Saving bees from pesticides and habitat loss starts with small choices. It becomes a real change when many people make them. items.title: Τι συμβαίνει με τα παλιά σας ρούχα; Μέσα σε ένα δίκτυο της Βομβάης που μετατρέπει 17500 κιλά σε εισόδημα για εμπόρους και τεχνίτες
items.titleOriginal: What Happens to Your Old Clothes? Inside a Mumbai Network Turning 17500 Kg Into Income for Traders & Artisans
items.description: «Μπαντιγουάλα, μπχαντιβάλα». Για χρόνια, η γνωστή κλήση ήταν μέρος του τρόπου με τον οποίο ο 35χρονος Anil Datanini κέρδιζε τα προς το ζην. Όπως και άλλοι bhandiwalas, μάζευε παλιά ρούχα, παραδοσιακά αντάλλαζε με σκεύη και πούλησε ό,τι μπορούσε να επαναχρησιμοποιηθεί. Είχε μπει στο εμπόριο γύρω στα 15, ακολουθώντας δουλειά που γνώριζε καλά η οικογένειά του. Αφού μετακόμισε από το Γκουτζαράτ στη Βομβάη, αυτός…
items.descriptionOriginal: "Bhandiwala, bhandiwala." For years, the familiar call was part of how 35-year-old Anil Datanini earned a living. Like other bhandiwalas , he collected old clothes , traditionally exchanged for utensils, and sold what could be reused. He had entered the trade at around 15, following work his family knew well. After moving from Gujarat to Mumbai, he continued sorting textiles and finding buyers for them. But there was one thing he could never count on: how much material he would find. Some days brought plenty of clothes; on others, hours spent looking for them yielded very little. That began to change in January 2026, when Anil partnered with Textile Waste Innovation Network (TWIN), a Mumbai-based enterprise founded by 29-year-old Vikram Shahi. Instead of sourcing everything himself, Anil now receives a more regular supply of used clothes, which he sorts, prepares and sells through markets in villages and rural areas. "Now the material comes to us regularly, so we can work properly," he says. "We sort it according to the quality and condition and then send the reusable clothes to villages." Anil says he currently earns between Rs 25,000 and Rs 30,000 a month, sometimes more. For him, the greater relief is being able to plan household expenses and save with more confidence. His experience captures an important part of TWIN's approach. According to its founder, the network has collected around 17,500 kg of used textiles and reached more than 650 households. It is doing so by working with waghari workers and bhandiwalas , whose experience in collecting and reselling clothes has long kept usable fabric in circulation. From his mother's cupboard to Mumbai's beaches When Vikram was growing up in Mumbai, he watched his mother exchange old clothes for steel utensils with a bhandiwala . He understood the exchange, but wondered what happened to those clothes afterwards. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. Born in Bihar, with family roots in Sitamarhi, Vikram moved to Mumbai with his parents when he was three. In 2017, while studying information technology at Mumbai University, he began volunteering at clean-up drives. At Versova beach that monsoon, he noticed clothes mixed in with the plastic waste. He saw more discarded textiles during subsequent clean-ups, including around festivals such as Holi. In 2019, he began organising drives of his own with support from Bhumi NGO. The question from his childhood returned: where did damaged clothes go when they were no longer useful to their owners? In 2022, Vikram enrolled for a master's in social work at the College of Social Work, Nirmala Niketan, Mumbai. A term paper on waste management helped him explore what happens to post-consumer textiles, meaning clothes and other fabrics discarded after use. "Post-consumer textile waste was not getting the kind of attention I felt it deserved," he tells The Better India . The gap became clearer in 2024, when he joined ReCircle as a sales executive. He had initially applied to work in plastic waste management, but was offered a role involving textiles instead. "At that point, I did not know much about textile waste, but once I started working on it, I realised there was a huge gap in the collection system," he says. People had familiar ways of passing on clothes that were still wearable: donating them, giving them to relatives or exchanging them for utensils. Torn T-shirts, worn-out bedsheets and other unusable fabric were more difficult to deal with. Even where recycling or upcycling options existed, there was no obvious route connecting a household's unwanted textiles to the people who could process them. A 1,200-kg experiment in the Mumbai monsoon In August 2025, while working full time on education initiatives, including STEM labs in schools, Vikram and a few friends organised a textile collection drive in Vasai. They gathered around 1,200 kg of material, despite heavy monsoon rain complicating the collection. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. "I was still working at the time, so we were doing this mostly on weekends," he recalls. "The first drive itself gave us confidence that people actually had this problem and were looking for a solution." TWIN was formally registered on 30 October 2025. Vikram continued his job until February 2026, when he began focusing on the enterprise full time. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "We are not trying to replace the existing recovery network. We are trying to build on it and create a more organised collection layer around it," he explains. What happens to clothes after TWIN collects them? TWIN collects used textiles from households, housing societies, schools, colleges, hotels, companies, NGOs and other bulk generators across the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Household pickups are described by the enterprise as free. A resident can request a collection through TWIN's website or WhatsApp chatbot, sharing their name, location and details of the textiles. The team records the request, including the quantity and type of material, in a customer relationship management system (CRM) before verifying it and assigning a collection partner. The enterprise works with waghari and bhandiwala workers, providing training, checking backgrounds and assigning collection areas by PIN code. This helps coordinate pickups that were previously handled more informally. The collected clothes are then sorted by condition, fabric and possible next use. That step determines whether a shirt can be worn again or whether a damaged bedsheet might be more useful as raw material for another product. He wanted to make textile collection easier for households while giving existing recovery workers a more dependable source of material. "Sorting is one of the most important parts because every textile cannot go to the same place," Vikram says. "We look at the condition, quality and what the next best use can be." Wearable clothes are prioritised for reuse. Workers sell them through their existing networks in villages and second-hand markets, where buyers, including farmers, can find affordable clothing. A smaller share goes to communities through NGO partners. Fabric unsuitable for wearing can take a different route. TWIN sends suitable material to upcycling partners, including The Kapda Project and artisan groups, to be made into bags, pouches and bottle holders. It also helps connect these products with buyers, including through organisations such as Sparkling Wings and Prayas Foundation. Lower-grade textiles may be downcycled into mats, rags or wiping cloths for industrial use. Recycling remains at the pilot stage, with TWIN and its partners testing which materials can be processed further. The network therefore offers several recovery routes, rather than claiming that every collected item becomes a new garment or recycled fibre. For residents, the idea is straightforward: clothes that have outlived their original use need different destinations. TWIN says it accepts wearable and torn clothes, bedsheets and curtains, but not wet or soiled material. That distinction matters when someone is clearing out a cupboard and wondering what can actually be collected. 'Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work' TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Some receive around 200 to 300 kg of sorted textiles from the warehouse in a week, while others collect material directly from households. TWIN currently works with around 15 to 20 informal textile recovery workers, of whom seven to 10 are connected to a more regular supply. Anil, who has lived in the Sion-Dharavi area, says this has changed how he organises his work. Earlier, much of his time went into finding textiles before he could begin sorting and selling them. Now he can spend more of it preparing clothes for buyers. "We had to go and search for clothes ourselves," he says. "Sometimes we would get material and sometimes we would not. The supply was not regular." For 22-year-old Bhavesh Dattani, the difference feels familiar. He grew up in Dharavi, where his family continued a clothes-trading livelihood after his grandparents moved from Gujarat. Before joining TWIN in December 2025, he went from neighbourhood to neighbourhood exchanging utensils for clothes. "The barter system takes a lot of time. We have to go from place to place and ask people for clothes, and we do not know how much we will collect," he says. Now, he receives reusable garments from the team. "Now we get clothes regularly, so there is more work and the income is also more regular," he adds. He does not specify his earnings, but says having material available more consistently has improved his working routine. Another worker, Vikram Shankar Chekhaliya, about 45, comes from a family in Gujarat that has worked with textiles for generations. Associated with the initiative since its early stages in July 2025, he had previously sourced, sorted and sold clothes independently, including lower-value fabric used for wiping. "Sometimes we would get good clothes, and sometimes there would be very little material. Now there is a regular supply, so it becomes easier to plan the work," he says. These workers already know how to assess clothing and where it can be sold. What TWIN is trying to add is a more predictable connection between the households discarding textiles and the markets that can use them. Who earns what when an old shirt is sold again? Although household pickups are free, the enterprise earns through the sale and recovery of collected material, as well as service-based work with organisations. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Reusable clothes move through existing traders and markets, allowing workers to earn from their sale. TWIN also generates revenue from recovered textiles. Upcycled products made by partner artisans create another income stream when they are purchased by organisations or corporate clients. Lower-grade materials can be sold for uses such as industrial wiping, while business-to-business services add to the model. "The idea is not just to collect waste and then store it," Vikram says. "There has to be a value chain after collection. We need to make sure the material moves to the right person or the right organisation and that there is a revenue stream to sustain the system." Vikram began with his own resources. TWIN has also received support from Mumbai Ekatra, a citizen-focused grant programme, particularly for its upcycling work. According to Vikram, the enterprise has generated about Rs 3 lakh in business revenue, with another Rs 3 lakh worth of potential business in the pipeline. It has yet to turn profitable, he says, with much of its income being put back into building the collection and sorting network. 17,500 kg of clothes collected. What comes next? The WhatsApp chatbot, launched in June 2026 after TWIN initially relied on Instagram and a Google Form, has made it easier to organise incoming requests. Vikram says it recorded more than 300 registrations in its first month. The team can also track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. Technology helps manage the movement of textiles, but the recovery itself still depends on people who know how to sort, repair, reuse or sell them. For now, the work is focused on Mumbai. Vikram hopes to expand to other cities, adapting the collection network to the workers, markets and waste patterns already present in each place. There are challenges ahead. Recycling is still being tested , the enterprise is not profitable and only part of its worker network currently receives a regular supply. The team can track where clothes are coming from, how much is collected and which partner should handle each pickup. But the model has begun to connect two needs that often sit apart: households looking for a responsible way to part with old textiles, and workers looking for material they can earn from. For Anil, that connection has a practical meaning. He still sorts clothes, finds buyers and does the work he has known since his teens. What has changed is the amount of time he needs to spend searching for the next batch, and the confidence that there will be work to return to. All pictures courtesy Vikram Shahi.

items.title: Το 1994, οι Oasis μήνυσαν για 500.000 δολάρια από την Coca-Cola για ένα τραγούδι που έμοιαζε πολύ με μια εμβληματική διαφήμιση
items.titleOriginal: In 1994, Oasis was sued for $500,000 by Coca-Cola for a song that sounded very similar to an iconic ad
items.description: Όπως λέει η παροιμία, «Όλοι οι μουσικοί είναι κλέφτες», και κανείς δεν έχει ανταποκριθεί στον τίτλο όπως οι βασιλιάδες της Britpop, οι Oasis. Το σπουδαίο είναι ότι δεν απολογούνται καθόλου για την αγάπη τους να αποτίουν φόρο τιμής σε άλλους καλλιτέχνες υψώνοντας τις μελωδίες, τα riff και τους στίχους τους. Η εισαγωγή στο πιάνο στο "Don't Look Back in Anger" μοιάζει με το "Imag" του John Lennon…
items.descriptionOriginal: As the adage goes, “All musicians are thieves,” and no one has lived up to the title quite like Britpop kings, Oasis. The great thing is that they are completely unapologetic about their love of paying tribute to other artists by lifting their melodies, riffs, and lyrics. The piano intro to “Don’t Look Back in Anger” sounds like John Lennon’s “Imagine.” The main riff to “Cigarettes and Alcohol” is “Bang a Gong” by T. Rex. The song “Step Out” sounded so much like “Uptight (Everything Is Alright)” by Steve Wonder that they took it off an album and made it a B-side. They still got sued by Wonder and his co-writers. The list goes on and on. It’s one thing to get sued by fellow musicians for repurposing their ideas, but in 1994, just after the release of their debut album Definitely Maybe , Oasis was sued by a major multinational corporation, Coca-Cola, for their second single “Shakermaker.” Not bad for 5 kids who grew up in working-class Manchester, England. Coca-Cola claimed that the band ripped off “I’d Like to Teach the World to Sing (In Perfect Harmony),” a song it used in an iconic 1971 ad campaign, and they most certainly did. In fact, in early concerts, the band sang lyrics to the song in the opening: I’d like to teach the world to sing In perfect harmony I’d like to buy the world a Coke And keep it company The band changed the lyrics to: I’d like to be somebody else And not know where I’ve been I’d like to build myself a house Out of plasticine The Coca-Cola ad was so popular that The New Seekers re-recorded the song and released it as a single that went to #1 . The ad was also a big part of the final episode of Mad Men , where ad exec Don Draper dreams up the ad in an enlightened state. “We ripped it off, so they had the right to sue us. Fair enough. People will steal from other bands but change the lyrics. We just did the same thing but kept some of the same lyrics in. We drink Pepsi now,” Oasis guitarist Paul “Bonedhead” Arthurs said, according to Far Out . There’s no doubt that Oasis stole the melody of the Coca-Cola song; they even admitted it. But “Shakermaker” was written in an era when artists often lifted ideas from older recordings and spun them into something fresh. Early ‘90s hip-hop was rooted in artists sampling older recordings and using melodies from hit songs in new, inventive ways. Oasis’ Manchester contemporaries, The Happy Mondays, openly stole music from The Beatles , LaBelle , and Donovan . “Shakermaker” was written by Oasis’ chief songwriter, Noel Gallagher, and features references to “Mr. Soft,” a character in a Trebor Soft Mints commercial that ran in the UK. The title references the Shaker-Maker , a ‘70s toy where children combined powder and water to mold tiny figures. By using the melody in an iconic ’70s TV ad, Noel Gallagher did more than steal a melody; he was referencing the disposable pop culture of his youth. “I don’t think I’ve ever actually re-written somebody else’s song,” Noel Gallagher told Access in 1997 . “I’ve put bits of other people’s songs into my songs, yeah. I stuck a little bit of ‘Imagine’ on the front of ‘Don’t Look Back In Anger’—but they’re not the same song, right? But if I do that, I don’t do it by accident; I do it on purpose.” The good news is that Coca-Cola and Oasis mended fences in 2011, when the beverage company used its 1994 song “Whatever” in an ad campaign to celebrate its 125th anniversary. Not shockingly, Oasis settled out of court with EMI after the song’s release because it sounded an awful lot like the “Seventh Member of Monty Python” Neil Innes’ song, “How Sweet to Be an Idiot.” The post In 1994, Oasis was sued for $500,000 by Coca-Cola for a song that sounded very similar to an iconic ad appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο Fred Astaire έκανε μια σχάρα καπέλων να μοιάζει με παρτενέρ χορού. Προσέξτε τη στιγμή που αφήνει να φύγει.
items.titleOriginal: Fred Astaire made a hat rack look like a dance partner. Watch the moment he lets go.
items.description: Οι περισσότεροι πιθανότατα γνωρίζουν τον Fred Astaire για τους άψογους χορούς του με αστέρια όπως ο Ginger Rogers και η Rita Hayworth. Αλλά ακόμα πιο εντυπωσιακό, μερικές από τις πιο εμβληματικές ρουτίνες του περιλάμβαναν έναν χορευτικό παρτενέρ που δεν ήταν καθόλου άνθρωπος. Χαρακτηριστική περίπτωση: η ρουτίνα του στη βάση καπέλων από το Royal Wedding . Στο μιούζικαλ του 1951, ο χαρακτήρας του Astaire, Tom Bowen, κάνει πρόβες ενώ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Most people probably know Fred Astaire for his flawless dances with stars like Ginger Rogers and Rita Hayworth. But even more impressive, some of his most iconic routines involved a dance partner who wasn’t human at all. Case in point: his hat rack routine from Royal Wedding . In the 1951 musical, Astaire’s character, Tom Bowen, is rehearsing while his dance partner and sister, Ellen, is absent. Sans a human partner, Astaire dances to “Sunday Jumps” using whatever happens to be around him, including an unassuming hat rack. In true Astaire form, he made this unlikely pairing come to life in the most magical way. Astaire doesn’t just dance with the hat rack It’s really not just that Astaire adeptly and gracefully moves around the room with this piece of furniture. It was his remarkable ability to commit to the idea that this rack was another performer. This gift was even noted in a recent academic study of the MGM musical , which commended Astaire for transforming the “inanimate object into a whirling ‘dervish’ of excitement that pirouettes on his every command because he gave it the same attention and focus he would give a “human dance partner.” Another way of putting it: Astaire wasn’t necessarily trying to convince the audience that the hat rack was a person. But he was, in his own way, offering the object the same level of respect that we would a person. In the routine, at least. Watch the moment he lets go To this point, there’s one particularly cool moment when Astaire gets the rack moving and releases it. For a beat, it keeps going without him. That sounds simple enough, until you consider what the audience has just been trained to see. Up until that point, Astaire has spent the routine establishing a rhythm between himself and the object. So when he lets go, the hat rack’s continued movement feels almost like a response. The Washington Post later described the sequence as a “pas de deux with a rack,” referring to the ballet term where the male dancer supports his partner with lifts, turns, and balances, allowing her to execute complex lines and extensions. Which may be the perfect description. Astaire had a particular talent for these kinds of solos. According to The Washington Post , an American Film Institute tribute in 1981, a retrospective of his work included solos in which he created “magic” with a golf club, drums, and other props-turned-partners. Decades later, the hat rack got a new partner The routine even had an unusual second life. In 1997, a Dirt Devil advertising campaign digitally altered footage from Royal Wedding so that Astaire appeared to dance with a vacuum cleaner instead of the hat rack. Producing the commercials required a dancer to recreate Astaire’s movements while holding the vacuum on a specially constructed set, which was then digitally combined with the original footage. The ads were…controversial . Astaire’s widow approved them. However, his daughter objected to the use of her father’s image. Regardless, this campaign demonstrated just how iconic the original choreography was. Because even with a Dirt Devil instead of a hat rack, the moves were instantly recognizable. Astaire is long gone, but his legacy continues to show that true star power lies not just in technical skills, but in the ability to make anyone, or anything, feel truly seen. items.title: Ένας 79χρονος πήγε σε σχολή ομορφιάς για να βοηθήσει την 50χρονη γυναίκα του. Η όρασή της εξασθενούσε.
items.titleOriginal: A 79-year-old went to beauty school to help his wife of 50 years. Her eyesight was failing.
items.description: Ένα ήσυχο απόγευμα του Απριλίου του 2021, ένας άνδρας γύρω στα 70 του χτύπησε την πόρτα του Delmar College of Hair & Esthetics στο Red Deer της Αλμπέρτα και ρώτησε αν προσέφεραν μαθήματα. «Είπα ότι το κάνουμε σίγουρα», είπε η σκηνοθέτις Carrie Hannah στο Red Deer News Now. Μετά εξήγησε γιατί ρωτούσε. Το όραμα της γυναίκας του πήγαινε και συνέχιζε να καίει τον εαυτό της…
items.descriptionOriginal: One quiet afternoon in April 2021, a man in his late 70s knocked on the door of Delmar College of Hair & Esthetics in Red Deer, Alberta, and asked whether they offered courses. “I said that we sure do,” director Carrie Hannah told Red Deer News Now . Then he explained why he was asking. His wife’s vision was going , and she kept burning herself with her curling iron . “He said, ‘I’d really like to be able to help her but I don’t know how,’” Hannah recalled. View this post on Instagram His wife of 50 years had always taken pride in her appearance, Hannah said, “and it’s important to her, so therefore important to him.” The school paired him with a student, Britney Smith, and a mannequin head. Over about an hour, she taught him to set volume curls on short hair and how to keep the hot iron away from his wife’s skin. Then he had one more request: his wife had been poking herself in the eye with her mascara wand. “He also asked for tips on applying mascara because that task was hard for her also, so we gave him a makeup lesson too!” Hannah told SWNS, according to People . Throughout the lesson, he kept pulling photos of his wife out of his wallet to show the room, from every age. “Bragging on what a beautiful and wonderful wife she is,” Hannah said. She’d been a courtroom stenographer who could type more than 100 words a minute. He even got a haircut himself before he left. Smith ( @hairdesignbybritney on Instagram) posted photos of the lesson on-line and they reached hundreds of thousands by the next morning. The man, who asked to stay anonymous, was turning 80 that May. “I think he is also a very brave man for stepping into a hair college and asking for lessons on styling hair,” Hannah said. “I don’t think too many men would do that.” A few weeks later, he came back to the school with his wife to say thank you. According to Hannah, they were both “impressed with his new professional skills, and her hair is looking great!” “It’s not always the big gestures,” she said. “He cares enough about her to come to a beauty school.” He’s in good company. In 2018, an Irish husband named Des Monahan learned to do his wife Mona’s makeup after her eyesight began to fail. The couple were regulars at their local Debenhams department store, and after watching a makeup artist get Mona ready for a party, Des decided he could do it himself. The post A 79-year-old went to beauty school to help his wife of 50 years. Her eyesight was failing. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: 1.000 Ελβετοί εθελοντές έθαψαν τα εσώρουχά τους για την επιστήμη. Μόλις κέρδισε ένα βραβείο Ig Nobel.
items.titleOriginal: 1,000 Swiss volunteers buried their underwear for science. It just won an Ig Nobel Prize.
items.description: Το 2021, περίπου 1.000 άνθρωποι σε όλη την Ελβετία έλαβαν ένα ασυνήθιστο πακέτο με το ταχυδρομείο: δύο ζευγάρια ολοκαίνουργια λευκά βαμβακερά εσώρουχα, μαζί με οδηγίες για να τα θάψουν. Ήταν ένα πρόγραμμα επιστήμης των πολιτών με το όνομα «Proof by Underpants», το οποίο διευθύνεται από το Πανεπιστήμιο της Ζυρίχης και το Agroscope, το ομοσπονδιακό κέντρο γεωργικής έρευνας της Ελβετίας. Η ιδέα ήταν sim…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2021, about 1,000 people across Switzerland got an unusual package in the mail: two pairs of brand-new white cotton underwear , along with instructions to bury them. It was a citizen science project called “ Proof by Underpants ,” run by the University of Zurich and Agroscope , Switzerland’s federal agricultural research center. The idea was simple. Bacteria, fungi, earthworms and other soil organisms eat cotton and the more life there is in a patch of ground, the faster a pair of underwear disappears. View this post on Instagram Volunteers buried more than 2,000 pairs, along with 12,000 tea bags, at roughly 1,000 sites around the country: private gardens, lawns, meadows and farm fields. Two months later, they dug them back up, photographed what was left and mailed the remains to the lab with soil samples. “People don’t realize that 50 percent of all living species live in the soil,” said Marcel van der Heijden, a University of Zurich professor who co-led the study. View this post on Instagram The results, published in August in the journal Plants, People, Planet , showed huge differences. Underwear buried in private gardens decomposed fastest, thanks to soil rich in organic matter and teeming with life. Underwear in lawns held up the best. Farm fields and meadows fell in between, and organic fields broke the cotton down faster than conventional ones. The biggest predictor wasn’t the soil’s chemistry, but what people did with the land. “Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a statement . View this post on Instagram That doesn’t mean faster is always better as the researchers noted that in some settings, like forests, extremely rapid decomposition can signal too many nutrients rather than healthy balance. But for most land, the advice was familiar stuff like keep the soil covered, add compost, rotate crops, and don’t go too crazy with synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. About 240 of the volunteers ended up listed as co-authors, and the data is being turned into a map of soil health across Switzerland. Instead of underwear, could they have used something like old T-shirts instead? Sure, van der Heijden told the Swiss news agency Keystone-SDA , but far fewer people would have paid attention. View this post on Instagram “We wanted to encourage as many people as possible to take part, so we deliberately chose a somewhat provocative and humorous approach,” he said. It worked well enough to win an Ig Nobel Prize , a satirical award for unusual and creative research that “first makes people laugh, then makes them think.” On Sept. 3, van der Heijden and his teammates, Agroscope’s Franz Bender, science journalist Atlant Bieri and Pia Viviani, accepted the prize in soil science in Zurich, the first time in the awards’ 35-year history that the ceremony was held outside the United States. Nobel laureate Michel Mayor handed them the trophy. The prize money was 10 trillion Zimbabwean dollars, worth about 6 cents in the United States. The team accepted it with a song about their buried underpants, then threw clean pairs into the audience. The post 1,000 Swiss volunteers buried their underwear for science. It just won an Ig Nobel Prize. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: For some, the idea of changing things we don’t like about ourselves seems insurmountable. Perhaps this is because we think we need to make giant, bold leaps for reinvention. In reality, we don’t actually need huge moves to make changes. A neuroscience expert explains there are tiny daily actions we can take in order to slowly but surely change who we are. In a clip posted to Instagram, neuroscience expert Tina Levinson ( @rewiredmanifor online) discusses ways in which we can slowly change whatever version of ourselves we’d like to improve. As she sits in a pink sweater with two small dogs biting on sticks in her lap, a chyron appears which reads: “If I wanted to become an unrecognizable version of myself six months from now, these are the five things I’d practice every day.” Tina, Neuroscience Coach, Instagram She adds, “I say this as a neuroscience coach who had to use these exact practices to rebuild my own life. And none of them are big. Because this is what I think we get completely wrong about becoming a different person. We focus on the giant transformation, when your brain is actually changing in these tiny, almost boring moments throughout the day.” Question just one thought First she suggests to “question just one thought.” She explains, “Because your brain hands you predictions all day long disguised as facts, right? ‘I can’t do this. This is gonna go badly. They’re gonna judge me.’ And instead of immediately believing it, I’d ask, ‘Do I actually know that?’ That one question creates a tiny gap between what your brain predicts and what you choose to do.” Regulate before responding For her second lifehack, Levinson suggests truly regulating one’s self before responding to a situation, comment or even thought. “This one is huge. Because trying to make a different decision from the exact same dysregulated state is freaking hard. Take three psychological sighs. A deep inhale and another sip at the top…and a long exhale. Take a walk around the block, whatever works for you. Just change the state and then make the decision.” Do one thing that the ‘old version’ of you would not do She explains the importance of this, as she claims, “this is where identity starts changing.” She gives examples. “Say no, ask for the thing, post the video, stop explaining yourself. Your brain needs evidence and you can tell yourself you’re becoming more confident all day long, but doing the scary thing gives your brain receipts.” Look for what ‘is’ working “Because your brain,” she says, “is constantly deciding what information deserves your attention. So if you spend all day long asking what’s wrong, congratulations! Your brain will become incredibly efficient at answering you. So I would train it to notice something else.” Keep one promise to yourself every single day Levinson makes it clear that for this tip, one shouldn’t over promise. “Not ten,” she says. “Just one. Because imagine giving your brain 180 straight days of evidence that says when I say I’m going to do something, I do it. So who are you after six months of that?” She winds down by reiterating how these tiny changes add up. “This is the part that I wish more people understood about changing their lives. You don’t become a different person and then start behaving differently. You start practicing different thoughts, different responses, different behaviors. And eventually your brain goes, ‘okay, this is who we are now.’ That is neuroplasticity. And that is how you create the life that you actually want.” Cognitive behavioral therapy Her ideas are similar to concepts found in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). In a recent article for Psychology Today, Seth J. Gillihan, PhD, reminds readers that this concept isn’t exactly new. “At least since the time of Greek philosopher Epictetus nearly 2000 years ago, we’ve known that ‘People are not disturbed by things but by the view they take of them.’ Is that idea any different from 20th-century cognitive therapy?” He continues, “Long before Emerson said to ‘Always do what you are afraid to do,’ humans have known that the best way to overcome our fears is to face them. The history of mindfulness goes back thousands of years to Buddhism and Hinduism, a long time before it was popularized as a non-religious Western practice.” The post Neuroscience expert explains 5 ways to become ‘unrecognizable’ 6 months from now appeared first on Upworthy .

Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Κατά τη διάρκεια τεσσάρων ημερών στην Ολυμπιακή Χερσόνησο της Ουάσιγκτον, είδα έναν Ολυμπιακό…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Phil Starks , an associate professor of biology at Tufts University, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . During four days on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, I saw an Olympic marmot , a species found nowhere else on Earth; four bumblebee species working the same lavender plant; three western hermit crab species new to me; and five orcas slicing through the dark water off Ediz Hook . Any one of them could have been the trip’s highlight. Yet the encounter I cannot stop talking about occurred at low tide at Tongue Point , when I heard a barnacle. While I had seen thousands of barnacles, I had never imagined I could hear one. It made a noise that sounded like: Clickety-clack. Clickety-clack. Pop. As a professor who teaches about animal behavior , I know that the distinction between encountering an animal and actually noticing what it is doing is one of the simplest ways into natural history . It requires no laboratory and, at first, no special expertise. Mostly it requires learning how to let something ordinary become interesting again. At Low Tide My habit in places like a rocky shore is to become still and let my vision soften. Instead of staring at one point, I allow movement anywhere in the visual field to pull my attention. At Tongue Point, I was thinking about the demands of life in the intertidal zone , the shore between high and low tide: temperature swings, desiccation, and the cost of remaining clamped shut in open air. Then I noticed the soundscape. At first, the clicking was just coastal noise. I attributed it to small shore crabs moving among the mussels, or hermit crab shells knocking against them. Then one sharp pop pulled my attention to a single acorn barnacle . Its tiny opening was slightly unsealed, and two small plates were moving against its deeply ridged shell. The movement appeared to coincide with another pop. Then another. The repetition gave me something to follow. You can train yourself to do this almost anywhere. Watch honeybees fly around and see what you notice. When I take students or my sons to watch honeybees , I tell them not to stare directly at the hive entrance. Instead, sit nearby, look toward the open sky, and relax your gaze. At first you see empty air. Then a bee crosses it. Then another. Within moments the emptiness becomes a busy airport of arrivals and departures. Nothing new has entered the scene. You have just changed what you are capable of noticing. A Web of Assumptions Observation has its own traps. Sometimes you can miss behavior because it blends into the background. Other times you see something perfectly but stop asking questions because somebody has already told you what it means. Orb-weaver spiders offer a good example . Some add conspicuous bands or patches of dense silk to their webs. These structures are called stabilimenta , a name inherited from the old idea that they stabilize or strengthen the web. But they don’t. Researchers later found evidence for several possible functions: attracting prey, deterring or confusing predators, protecting webs from larger animals, and, in some cases, helping with temperature regulation. Different functions may matter in different species, environments, or stages of life. Muhammad Mahdi Karim/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA This orb-weaver rests on the stabilimentum of its web. I first became interested in the debate over stabilimentum function because I was unconvinced that one explanation could account for all the evidence. I started out asking whether somebody was wrong. The better question turned out to be why researchers expected one universal answer in the first place. That remains one of my favorite lessons from animal behavior: A name can be useful, but it can also sneak in an explanation. Once you think you know what something is, you become less likely to watch what it actually does. Seeing Isn’t Knowing The opposite mistake is just as easy: seeing something interesting and immediately deciding you understand it. After I returned from the Olympic Peninsula, I emailed a retired marine invertebrate zoologist and described what I had seen and heard. His response was delighted and appropriately skeptical: “Doubt it. Take a short video next time.” Aleria Jensen/NOAA/NMFS/AKFSC via Flickr How would you confirm these barnacles made a sound? I saw an open barnacle move and heard a pop at the same time. That is an observation. I did not demonstrate that the barnacle produced the sound. A mussel bed contains crabs, moving shells, and a host of other possible sources. A close-up video with synchronized audio could test whether the same visible movement repeatedly coincided with each pop. Noticing something is the start of science. It does not let you skip the work that follows. Look Again For anyone who wants to become a better naturalist , a simple sequence helps: Notice something. Describe it carefully. Ask what else could explain it. Decide what evidence would distinguish among those possibilities. Try it somewhere familiar: a backyard, city park, pond edge, patch of flowers, or shoreline. Stay longer than feels necessary. Let the sights and sounds become background. Then look for repetition. One movement, then another like it. One sound that separates from the rest. An animal returning to the same place. And once something catches your attention, resist the urge to explain it too quickly. Watch again. You may discover something genuinely unusual. More likely, you will discover something ordinary that you had never actually seen before. I may not have witnessed rare behavior at Tongue Point or identified a rare species. But I stayed long enough to wonder what I was hearing. Maybe that was rare enough. RELATED: What Are the Mysterious Creatures Quacking Under the Sea? We’re a Step Closer to Finding Out

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Maybe you’ve noticed it creeping in over the last few weeks. You finish lunch, and an hour later you’re already drifting back toward the kitchen. The bowl of soup that would have filled you up in May barely makes a dent, and somewhere around four o’clock you’d trade almost anything for a warm slice of something with cinnamon on top. It’s easy to blame the pumpkin bread and cider doughnuts suddenly everywhere you look, and they’re certainly not helping. But if you’ve been feeling hungrier in the fall, there’s more going on than seasonal temptation. Your body is responding to shorter days, colder air, and some very old instincts, all at the same time. Registered dietitian Lyndsay Hall of JM Nutrition walked through what’s behind that bigger appetite, and the good news is that none of it means you’re doing anything wrong. Why you feel hungrier in the fall Old instincts that haven’t caught up For most of human history, the end of summer meant leaner months were coming. “For those living in colder climates, fall signifies the transition from summer to winter, when historically food access would have been limited in the coming months, so people would eat more and put on some extra weight intentionally to help them get through the cold winter season,” Hall said. Your grocery store stays stocked all year, of course, but your body doesn’t know that. Like animals building up reserves before hibernation, some of that seasonal pull toward eating more may be wiring we’ve carried with us for a very long time. Staying warm takes energy Cold weather asks more of you physically, too. “When we start to feel physically cold, our bodies will expend more energy trying to keep us warm (i.e., by shivering) and diverting more blood flow to organs to keep them up and running,” Hall said. More energy spent means your body sends stronger signals to refuel. Less sunlight, shifting moods Then there’s the light, or the lack of it. “Many people experience a drop in serotonin levels during the fall and winter months due to decreased sun exposure and the cold weather making it difficult to get outside as often as we might during the summer months,” Hall said. Lower serotonin can affect hunger and fullness cues, making cravings stronger and meals feel less satisfying. For some people, the darker months bring more than a mild case of the winter blues . If low mood, fatigue, or changes in appetite start to feel heavy or stick around, it’s a good idea to check in with a doctor, since seasonal affective disorder is common and very treatable. Holidays on the horizon Fall also kicks off the stretch of the year when so many gatherings revolve around food. “Over time, we have created psychological associations between certain times of year and eating more or indulging. Thanksgiving, for example, occurs in the fall months and is often centered around eating that many look forward to,” Hall said. The same goes for Christmas, Hanukkah, Kwanzaa and New Year’s, when the dishes on the table tend to be rich, hearty and tied up with memories. Staying satisfied through fall and winter None of this calls for a diet or a calorie tracker. Hall’s approach is to lean on three things that help meals stick with you longer: protein, fiber, and healthy fats. “Protein and fiber help to keep us physically satiated for longer periods of time,” she said. Together with fats, they slow digestion, so a cozy meal keeps you going well into the afternoon. Fold protein into the comfort foods you love Hall suggests stirring Greek yogurt or cottage cheese, or a high-protein plant-based alternative, into muffin batter, pancakes, and quick breads. A splash of milk or a dairy-free version in your oatmeal or morning latte works the same way. Eggs, tofu, fish and poultry can round out casseroles and pasta bakes, too. Let vegetables and legumes do the heavy lifting Soups, stews and chilis are perfect for this. Skin-on potatoes, winter squash, eggplant, peppers, leafy greens and green beans add fiber without changing the spirit of a dish, and apples or pomegranate seeds bring a bright, seasonal crunch to salads. “Beans, chickpeas and lentils are great ways to add both protein and lots of fiber to soups, stews, chilis and stuffed vegetables,” Hall said. Give seasonal baking a fiber boost Seasonal treats can pull a little more weight, too. “Oat bran, chia, ground flaxseed, grated zucchini or carrot, and dried fruits can be easy sources of extra fiber for any baked good or hot cereals,” Hall said. So the next time your stomach rumbles an hour after lunch on a gray November afternoon, you can take it as your body doing what it’s long been built to do. Answer it with something warm and filling, save room for the dishes that only come around once a year, and let the season be one you enjoy at the table instead of second-guessing every bite. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary .
