Το χάπι του Αλτσχάιμερ, αναπτύξτε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A once-daily tablet called AR1001 slowed cognitive decline by 31 percent over a year in people with early Alzheimer’s disease who were not on any other Alzheimer’s medication, according to phase 3 results presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. The Alzheimer’s pill, developed by South Korean company AriBio, belongs to the same drug family as Viagra. Across the full trial population, which included patients already taking other Alzheimer’s drugs, the effect did not reach statistical significance. How the Alzheimer’s pill works A PDE5 inhibitor, not an amyloid drug AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitor. Drugs in this class relax blood vessels, which is how they work for erectile dysfunction, and for the brain the effect is increased blood flow. Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the mechanism likely goes beyond circulation. “This drug acts through boosting blood flow and likely also directly stimulating pathways in brain cells that promote learning and memory ,” she said. That sets it apart from the disease-modifying treatments that have come through late-stage trials in recent years, which target amyloid, the protein that builds up into plaques in the brains of people with Alzheimer’s. Dr. Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK , called AR1001 “especially interesting” for that reason. “Rather than targeting amyloid, it acts on a specific enzyme and influences several other processes involved in brain function ,” she said. A tablet instead of an infusion The format matters too. Existing disease-modifying options require infusions or injections, while AR1001 is swallowed once a day. Dr. Richard Oakley, associate director of research and innovation at Alzheimer’s Society, said that difference “could make treatment simpler.” Phase 3 trial results in detail 13 countries, 604 key participants The phase 3 trial, known as Polaris-AD , enrolled patients with early Alzheimer’s across 13 countries, including the UK. The headline result comes from the 604 participants who were taking no other Alzheimer’s drugs, a group in which the decline in memory and thinking slowed by nearly a third compared with placebo. “Over the year of the trial, this drug was able to effectively slow down people’s decline in memory and thinking by nearly a third, and the side-effects reported were mostly mild to moderate,” Oakley said. The subgroup question The catch is in the wider group. Among patients who were also taking existing medications for Alzheimer’s symptoms, AR1001 did not produce a statistically significant benefit, which means the trial missed significance across its full population. Scales acknowledged as much. “The trial demonstrated a statistically significant slowing of clinical decline in participants who were not taking other commonly used Alzheimer’s medications alongside the trial drug. However, this benefit was not significant across the overall trial group,” she said. Oakley said the reason for that gap needs further investigation. Next steps for a new Alzheimer’s treatment Regulators and further trials None of the experts treated the results as final. All called for additional trials, and the findings still need review by independent scientists and drug regulators before AR1001 could be prescribed. Oakley also warned against improvising with existing drugs. “AR1001 is from the same family of medicines as Viagra, but it is being developed specifically for Alzheimer’s disease,” he said, adding that people should not take Viagra to try to treat the condition. A different route against dementia The stakes are large. Alzheimer’ s is the most common form of dementia, and dementia is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050, with no cure available. Scales described the results as “an important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments,” and Oakley said they were “an exciting sign that we could have a totally new treatment for early Alzheimer’s disease that tackles its causes, not just its symptoms.” If larger studies confirm the effect and explain why it disappeared in patients on other medications, a daily tablet working through blood flow would give doctors a second line of attack alongside the amyloid drugs. items.descriptionOriginal: During the 1920s , radios had a boom in the United States. Sales of radios went from $60 million in 1922 to $426 million in 1929, according to the University of Houston Digital History . Families began to gather around their radios and listen to comedies, musical variety shows and news. And the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Home Economics and Farm Radio Service decided to create its own 15-minute broadcast aimed at housewives and all things homemaking in a number of different segments. The show, called Housekeeper Chat , centered on the fictional character Aunt Sammy, the wife of Uncle Sam (the famous United State’s federal government persona). It premiered on October 4, 1926. Aunt Sammy’s radio segments, explained The 15-minute Housekeeper Chat show was broken down into three, 5-minute segments: “Backyard Gossip”, “Questions Women are Asking”, and “What Shall We Have For Dinner?”. Real women took on the role of Aunt Sammy, including: Ruth Van DeMan , a home economics specialist who created many of Aunt Sammy’s recipes and menus; Josephine Hemphill , a journalism teacher who graduated from of Kansas State Agricultural College, who wrote many of the conversational scripts; and Fanny Walker Yeatman, who both tested and tasted recipes that were created for the show by the Bureau of Home Economics. Final show approvals were run through another woman, Dr. Louise Stanley, head of the Bureau of Home Economics, before the show aired. Ruth Van DeMan told a newspaper in 1927, “This is no caviar and truffle service for jazz-jaded appetites. We are striving to serve that great substantial class of women who are homemakers. We aim to make the menus simple and balanced.” Aunt Sammy’s Radio Recipes cookbook Housekeeper Chat was a hit. Demand for a cookbook featuring Aunt Sammy’s recipes and menus came flooding in, and the USDA compiled a cookbook that featured 70 favorite menus and 300 recipes from the show into Aunt Sammy’s Radio Recipes . And 100,000 copies of it were distributed between October 1926 and December 1927. In 1927, a million housewives were tuning in to the hit radio show. And the broadcast survived through the Great Depression, and was renamed to Homemaker Chats after 1934. It was discontinued in 1946, according to the University of North Texas . Photograph of Ruth Van DeMan preparing for the broadcast. Photo Courtesy: National Archive A 1931 recipe from ‘Aunt Sammy’s Radio Recipes’ A 1931 copy of Aunt Sammy’s Radio Recipes Revised is available through South Dakota State University . (You can also try making more original recipes shared back in 1927 in Aunt Sammy’s Radio Recipes: The Original 1927 Cookbook and Housekeeper’s Chat .) Here’s how to make an original recipe 1931 created by Ruth Van DeMan and Fanny Walker Yeatman for a seasonal treat, Cranberry Muffins. Cranberry Muffins 1 egg 3/4 cup milk 1/2 teaspoon salt 4 tablespoons melted butter or other fat 2 cups sifted flour 4 teaspoons baking powder 1/4 cup sugar. 1 cup cranberries Beat the egg slightly and add the milk. To the liquid mixture, add the sifted dry ingredients. Roll the berries in two more tablespoons of sugar, and fold into the batter with the melted fat. Do not stir the mixture any more than necessary. Pour into greased muffin pans and bake in a moderately hot oven (400°F.) for about 30 minutes, or until brown. Serve hot. items.titleOriginal: Before Natalie Imbruglia sang ‘Torn,’ its songwriter recorded a version with a very different bite
items.description: Κανένα soundtrack της δεκαετίας του 1990 δεν θα ήταν πλήρες χωρίς το "Torn" της Natalie Imbruglia. Το επιτυχημένο σινγκλ ήταν ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα τραγούδια της δεκαετίας του '90, καθώς ήταν στην κορυφή των ραδιοφωνικών charts για 11 εβδομάδες. Αναγνωρίζεται ευρέως ως ένα από τα πιο δημοφιλή και πιο επιδραστικά ποπ τραγούδια ποτέ. Το άγκιστρο ήταν πιασάρικο, η αυστραλιανή φωνή της Imbruglia ήταν μοναδική και μολυσματική και οι στίχοι…
items.descriptionOriginal: No soundtrack of the 1990s would be complete without Natalie Imbruglia’s “Torn.” The hit single was one of the biggest songs of the 90s, topping the radio charts for 11 weeks. It’s widely recognized as one of the most popular and influential pop songs ever. The hook was catchy, Imbruglia’s Australian voice was unique and infectious, and the lyrics were relatable to anyone who’d ever been disillusioned or felt alone even inside of a romantic relationship. The song was so popular, in fact, that it charted all over the world. “Torn” was a hit in Canada, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, and more. Truly iconic. Imbruglia’s “Torn” was, surprisingly, a cover What many people don’t realize about the song that immediately evokes all things 90s is that Imbruglia was not the original songwriter or even performer of “Torn.” “Torn” was written by Anne Preven along with Scott Cutler and Phil Thornalley in 1991, a full six years before Imbruglia’s version was released. Preven and Cutler were members of the California rock band Ednaswap. Ednaswap’s version of “Torn” was wildly different from the version many of us have grown to love. Instead of the lighthearted, whimsical music backing the lyrics and a synthetic beat, Ednaswap performed the song with guitars and heavy drums. Preven’s voice brought a completely different flavor to the lyrics, as well, as she infused it with far more grit; giving the song a mood of anger and frustration, along with a little bit of an edge. Even Ednaswap was not the first to record “Torn” Preven and her bandmates, along with Phil Thornalley, wrote “Torn” in 1991 but did not immediately record it. Instead, the song’s first recording went to Danish artist Lis Sørensen in 1993. Her version was a smash hit in Denmark about four years before Imbruglia recorded hers. But wait, the journey of this incredible song was not nearly over yet. Ednaswap finally recorded their own version of the song they wrote, adding it to their 1995 self-titled album. Meanwhile, the song was still busy making its way around the world. In 1996, singer Trine Rein released her own cover of “Torn” on her album Beneath My Skin . Each of these artists brought something a little different to the piece. Unique musical styles, vocal choices, and tones helped transform the meaning of the song for listeners all over the world. Finally, in 1997, Imbruglia’s version took the world by storm and became the international sensation we know today. But the staying power of the song is seen in the fact that it continues to be covered again and again. Bands and artists like Phoebe Bridgers and Neck Deep have put their own spin on “Torn.” And, famously, the band One Direction covered “Torn” for their very first performance on The X Factor , a showing that helped propel them to stardom. Who knew that such a simple, yet beautifully written, song could have such a lasting impact in pop culture all over the globe? 90s culture, even today’s pop music, might have been permanently altered for the better by a little known band and a trio of incredible songwriters. items.descriptionOriginal: Dr. Frankenstein learned the hard way that he couldn’t piece together a human to his own liking. But centuries later, it seems that people haven’t quite figured that out. “Frankensteining” is a buzzy term for attempting to mold your significant other into your idea of a perfect partner, rather than embracing their own unique personality. While this version might not be quite as messy as what’s depicted in the Mary Shelley novel, experts agree it doesn’t exactly lead to a healthy relationship. Upworthy spoke with several relationship experts about what “Frankensteining” looks like, why people do it, and how to tell when a desire for change has crossed a line. Here’s what they had to say. What “Frankensteining” looks like As Dr. Karen Stewart, Psy.D. notes, this behavior is “nothing new.” Unrealistic relationship expectations, perfectionism, or a need for control in a relationship can cause someone to fall in love with their partner’s potential rather than who they actually are. “Frankensteining often starts subtly and can even be disguised as love or concern,” she warns, “such as encouraging your partner to dress differently, lose weight, change their social circle, become more ambitious, or adopt your interests.” She adds that “individually, these suggestions may seem harmless, but over time, they can create a dynamic where one partner feels they are constantly being evaluated or corrected.” What “Frankensteining” is not Frankensteining is different from asking that a partner change a specific behavior (example: “Can you text me if you’ll be late?”), which couples communication coach Amber Frazier-Finkelstein notes is “normal.” Conversely, a demand like “I need you to be more ambitious” or “I wish you were more outgoing” is essentially asking a partner “to rewrite who they are.” In other words, there is a difference between asking a partner to treat you well and asking them to be a completely different person. How to spot the difference According to Dr. Natalie Harvey, LPC-S , a licensed therapist, a good way to tell if you’re “Frankensteining” in a relationship is to ask yourself three questions: Am I responding to who this person is, or to who I need them to be so I feel secure? Have they asked me for this input? If they never changed in this area, would I honestly stay? “It is kinder to accept someone as they are, or to leave honestly, than to stay and redesign them,” she added. Additionally, if you suspect your partner is “Frankensteining” you, Dr. Stewart says you can reflect on these questions: Do I feel supported in who I am currently, and what would it be like if I didn’t make these changes? What does it feel like when I say no to their suggestions? Ultimately, a healthy relationship doesn’t require either person to become someone else. People can grow together, compromise, and work on behaviors that affect the relationship. But again, there’s a big difference between supporting someone’s growth and trying to rebuild them in your own image. And if the person you’re with consistently falls short of the version you’ve imagined in your head, that may be worth paying attention to. Sometimes the more loving choice isn’t figuring out how to change someone. It’s recognizing that they’re already a whole person, and deciding whether the person they are is the person you want to love. The post People are ‘Frankensteining’ their partners. Therapists explain what that actually means. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Standing on stage in front of a crowd is already terrifying for many people. But being in the spotlight, with all eyes on you, and making a big mistake? Total nightmare fuel. Unless you’re Ella Fitzgerald, who turned an on-stage oopsies into an award-winning triumph. The iconic jazz singer took the stage in Berlin, Germany , on February 13, 1960, to sing “Mack the Knife.” But partway through the song, she completely blanked on the lyrics. She didn’t miss a beat Did Ella panic? Nope. She just kept right on singing the tune with the first words that came to her head: Oh, what’s the next chorus to this song now? This is the one now, I don’t know But it was a swingin’ tune and it’s a hit soon So we tried to do Mack the Knife She kept going in this improvised fashion for nearly two minutes, conjuring lyrics out of thin air. The most impressive part was that the words not only matched the tune and rhythm of the song, but many of them even fit the rhyme scheme. She even joked about her own flub-up within the impromptu lyrics, referencing Bobby Darin and Louis Armstrong, who originally made the song popular: Oh, Bobby Darin and Louis Armstrong They made a record, oh, but they did And now Ella, Ella and her fellas We’re makin’ a wreck, what a wreck of Mack the Knife That live flub-up won her a Grammy Ella Fitzgerald was a global sensation at this point in her career, so maybe audiences would have forgiven the hiccup even if she’d stopped and restarted the song. But the fact that she didn’t skip a beat simply solidified her status as a musical icon. Of course, it also helps that she was a jazz singer. In addition to the freestyle lyrics, she also filled the parts of the song where she had no words with nonsense syllables, a jazz technique known as scatting. Ella was famous for that kind of improvisation. The audience got a kick out of the performance, and the live recording of the song ended up earning her a Grammy for Best Female Vocal Performance (Single) in 1961. She also won Best Vocal Performance Album (Female) for the Mack the Knife—Ella in Berlin album. What made Ella Fitzgerald such a legend Ella Fitzgerald’s voice was nothing if not unique. But her voice didn’t just stand out for its unique sound. She could sing three full octaves (well above average, even for trained singers), and her voice has been described as “flexible, wide-ranging, accurate and ageless.” She could imitate every instrument in the orchestra, and she sang alongside the world’s greatest jazz musicians. Her audience was equally wide-ranging. She sang everywhere from small venues early in her career to world-renowned opera houses as she rose to global fame. People of all ages, races, and nationalities, rich or poor, loved to hear her sing. While she was somewhat self-conscious and reserved in her private life, she was fearless when she took the stage. “Once up there, I felt the acceptance and love from my audience,” Ella said. “I knew I wanted to sing before people the rest of my life.” And that she did. In her lifetime, Ella Fitzgerald won 13 Grammy awards, sold over 40 million albums, and was dubbed “The First Lady of Song.” No wonder she could recover from a forgotten lyric so quickly and turn it into an award-winning performance. Η Cross είχε καταγράψει τα συναισθήματά της για την αλλαγή της δυναμικής στην καριέρα της και το wi…
items.descriptionOriginal: Joan Cross spent 20 years as a passionate art teacher for K-8 grades in the Lakes Region of New Hampshire. But after a noticeable slide in student behavior and other teaching challenges, she decided to make a major career move: to become a commercial truck driver . Cross had been documenting her feelings about changing dynamics in her career and with her students in a personal audio diary. “It was helpful to make those recordings instead of writing things down,” shared in a 2023 interview with New Hampshire Public Radio . Cross offered more details on her audio diary and her decision to leave education for truck driving. “I’m not a school counselor. I’m not a psychologist,” she told NHPR’s Morning Edition host Rick Ganley. “And it felt like those were skills that I needed in order to get through my school day instead of just teaching art.” Cross’s career as an art teacher in changing times In one profound audio diary entry, Cross said: “I’ve spent thousands of dollars and thousands of hours to be an educator. I have a master’s degree. I’ve been doing this for 20 years, and I don’t recognize my profession anymore. Just the social-emotional skill level of these students is unrecognizable. “ Cross added that her classroom and the focus on making art was “falling apart”, noting that following the COVID-19 pandemic, behavioral issues were magnified. “[They were] having emotional issues. I’d have kids wailing, or I’d have kids that are growling at me, literally growling,” Cross added. “They will wreck a room, they’ll just flip a table. And I’m not equipped to help them.” For Cross, choosing to become a truck driver was partly due to diminishing classroom behavior, financial reasons, and overall lack of teacher support. “The pay is not keeping up with the cost of living,” she also shared. “Every time budget season came around, I would glibly be like, ‘Can I have an assistant?’ I need somebody to do all my office work, and all my email correspondence, and help me hang art shows, and label student work and student charts and grades. There’s all this clerical stuff that teachers are doing besides teaching.” Transitioning to truck driving Cross took matters into her own hands. “I earned my Commercial Driver License in 2022 in pursuit of a career change,” Cross wrote on LinkedIn . “My overarching professional goals are: driving a vehicle from a well-maintained fleet in a positive and efficient working environment where safety comes before schedule.” Cross told NHPR that she also decided to pursue her commercial license after growing up driving with her father. “My dad was a retired firefighter, and I just loved any time I got to go on the truck with him,” she explained. “And I like to drive big things.” Much like teaching, being a truck driver also offered Cross an opportunity to serve her community. “[With] teaching you get to serve the community. And whether you’re driving a bus or you’re driving freight, you are helping that community,” she added. “And that is a really, really important piece of my work life.” According to her LinkedIn, she left teaching in June 2023. She went on to train to become a bus driver as a Transit Operator Trainee for Manchester Transit Authority. And as of January 2024, she has been a Transit Driver for the Concord Area Transit (CAT). items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Reading Time: 2 minutes Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? Picture a weekend camping trip where your devices stay charged, your food stays fresh, and you have everything you need to enjoy a comfortable escape, all without using more energy than necessary. It might sound like a balancing act, but sustainable outdoor living is becoming easier thanks to smarter technology and a few simple changes in how we use energy. Whether you love camping, traveling in an RV, or entertaining in your backyard, your energy habits can have a bigger environmental impact than you might realize. Fortunately, reducing that impact doesn’t have to mean giving up the little comforts that make spending time outdoors so enjoyable. Make Better Use Of Natural Resources Nature already provides some of the resources you need to enjoy outdoor living comfortably. Making the most of natural daylight, for example, can significantly reduce your reliance on artificial lighting. Try planning outdoor activities around daylight hours and positioning your campsite or seating area to maximize natural light. When evening arrives, solar-powered lanterns and energy-efficient LED lights can provide illumination without consuming large amounts of electricity. Solar technology has also made it easier to generate electricity in remote locations, allowing you to enjoy modern conveniences while reducing your dependence on traditional power sources. Choose Smarter Ways To Power Your Adventures Keeping your essential equipment running is often one of the biggest challenges of spending extended periods outdoors. From charging smartphones to powering portable refrigerators, reliable electricity can make your adventures much more comfortable. However, not every activity requires a large generator or constant access to mains electricity. Portable power stations, rechargeable batteries, and solar-compatible equipment can offer practical alternatives. Looking at the equipment available from Power and Pedal can help you find power solutions suited to different outdoor activities . Choosing equipment that matches your energy requirements can reduce unnecessary consumption while ensuring you have sufficient power when you need it. Think Carefully About Your Outdoor Equipment It’s easy to accumulate gadgets and appliances when you enjoy outdoor activities, but not everything needs to be powered by electricity. For example, a well-insulated cooler might be sufficient for a weekend trip, eliminating the need for an electric refrigerator. Similarly, investing in quality thermal clothing and blankets can help you stay comfortable during cooler evenings without relying heavily on electric heating. When electrical equipment is necessary, prioritize energy-efficient models and maintain them properly to extend their lifespan. Plan Ahead To Avoid Wasting Energy Good preparation is one of the simplest ways to improve your outdoor energy habits. Charging devices before leaving home, downloading entertainment for offline use, and checking equipment before traveling can reduce unnecessary power consumption. Planning meals carefully can also help. Preparing ingredients in advance and choosing dishes that require less cooking time can reduce fuel use, especially on longer camping trips. Make Sustainability Part Of Your Outdoor Lifestyle Creating a more sustainable outdoor lifestyle doesn’t require dramatic changes. Often, it’s the smaller decisions that make the greatest difference when repeated consistently. By making thoughtful equipment choices, using renewable energy where practical, and avoiding unnecessary waste, you can reduce your environmental footprint without compromising your enjoyment. The goal isn’t to eliminate energy use entirely. It’s to use the energy you need more efficiently, allowing you to enjoy comfortable outdoor adventures while taking better care of the natural spaces you love exploring. The post Could Smarter Energy Habits Make Outdoor Living More Sustainable? appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Data from 10,000 workers show sit-stand desks boost active work time by 43 minutes a day—or roughly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. Every workday is a negotiation between our bodies and our jobs. Sit too long, our backs and necks protest; stand too long, our feet might have something to say about it. Sit-stand desks, also known as height-adjustable desks or standing desks, promise a healthier way to work, giving employees the flexibility to alternate between sitting and standing throughout the day. Now, new research suggests these desks may be giving employees, and employers, another benefit beyond ergonomics and well-being: productivity. Drawing on data from more than 10,000 employees, researchers at Texas A&M University found that workers who used sit-stand desks averaged 43 additional minutes of active computer use each day compared with those using regular desks, a difference that could translate to nearly $9,000 in annual productivity per employee. The study, published in Theoretical and Applied Ergonomics , was co-led by Texas A&M School of Public Health professor Mark Benden and US Army Public Health Command Region, West, Regional Ergonomist Tricia Salzar. The findings suggest that the physical workspace may be a powerful, often overlooked, influence on employee well-being, productivity, and even a company’s overall performance. When organizations look to boost performance and productivity, they turn to new technologies, training programs and management strategies. But another powerful influence may be hiding in plain sight: the physical workplace itself. “It’s what we call the ‘workplace effect,'” Benden says. “The direct impact that the physical work environment has on the behavior, health, psychological well-being, and even engagement and performance of employees.” Sit-stand desks are a striking example of the workplace effect. Rather than locking employees into a single position for hours at a time, they give workers the flexibility to sit, stand and move throughout the day, as tasks and energy levels shift. “It can have a profound effect,” Benden says. “Alternating between different working positions promotes better health outcomes by reducing physical strain and encouraging movement for those who might otherwise spend most of their workday sedentary.” But the benefits may extend beyond physical health. Benden and Salzar’s new research shows that sit-stand desks can also have a substantial impact on productivity. “It has a cumulative, positive effect for both employers and employees,” Benden says. For employees, height-adjustable desks could lead to sustained energy and longer stretches of focused work. For employers, the higher work productivity could translate into a nearly $9,000 return on investment per employee annually. “The implications are hard to ignore,” Benden says. “When we design workplaces around employees and their needs, better health, better performance and better organizational outcomes follow.” The takeaway? Investing in the physical workplace, like height-adjustable desks, isn’t just good for employee comfort and health; it could be good for business, too. To test whether sit-stand desks could influence work output and productivity, Benden and his colleagues stepped out of their labs and turned to the real world, using a resource few ergonomics studies can match. “We analyzed a huge dataset of more than 10,000 workers over a yearlong period, comparing the total computer use of traditional desk users and height-adjustable desk users,” Benden says. The records paired employee comfort surveys with a digital trail of workplace activity, tracking everything from keystrokes and words typed to mouse clicks and typing errors, all to paint a detailed picture of how employees interacted with their computers throughout the workday. “It was important that we collected subjective measurements, like employee survey responses of their comfort and objective measurements of computer activity through software, to analyze how people engaged with their work,” Benden says. The team found that workers with sit-stand desks averaged 3.66 hours of active computer time, compared with 2.95 hours among regular-desk employees—a gap of about 43 minutes a day. That might not sound like much, but over a year it adds up to roughly 171 additional hours, or more than four 40-hour workweeks. And those additional hours come with a practical price tag, too. Multiplying the 171 additional hours by a standardized hourly wage of about $52, the researchers estimate that sit-stand desks could generate nearly $9,000 in potential annual productivity value per employee. “Our findings were exciting because they suggest that height-adjustable desks can directly influence overall work output and economic organizational productivity,” Benden says. The researchers also found that employees using sit-stand desks generally typed more words and logged more keystrokes than their counterparts at non-adjustable desks. “The data showed that people aren’t just engaging with their work, they are producing output in a meaningful way,” Benden says. For Benden, the findings open the door to broader questions about the future of organizations, focusing on another force rapidly reshaping the modern workplace. “Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly integrated into daily work,” Benden says. “Just as we’ve studied how the physical environment affects human health and performance, we’re interested in understanding how emerging AI technologies could influence the physical workspace and outcomes of organizations.” From adjustable desks to emerging technologies, the underlying question remains the same: how can organizations design environments and systems to better support the people who use them? “The next breakthrough may not come from working harder, but from designing workspaces and systems that help people work smarter and more efficiently,” Benden says. The story told by the more than 10,000 employees is that the desk may be doing far more than just holding up your computer. For Benden, sit-stand desks represent more than an ergonomic innovation. They’re part of a lifelong passion to understand how workplaces can be designed to better support employee well-being and organizational success. “We spend a lot of time at work,” Benden says. “It’s my passion to make sure that workers feel supported in their workplace, built on informed and guided scientific evidence.” A former Army Reserve officer, engineer, healthcare professional, inventor and world-renowned researcher, Benden has spent decades studying the complex relationship between people and the environments in which they work. So, the next time you find yourself slumping in your chair at 3pm with an aching back, don’t just reach for another cup of coffee, because the verdict is in: show this study to your boss. items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia **184 trees face the axe in Mumbai. Thousands have objected. But is anyone listening?** 🌳 In Mumbai's Versova, residents once transformed a garbage dump into Nana Nani Park, reclaiming a neglected space and turning it into a green haven for the community. Today, that same park faces an uncertain future, with the proposed felling of **184 trees despite thousands of objections**. At a time when Mumbai is debating the future of its urban green spaces, Bhutan offers a powerful example of what sustainable development can look like. Recognised at the Earthshot Prize ceremony in Mumbai, Bhutan has made environmental conservation central to its vision of progress. Its Constitution mandates that **at least 60% of the country's land remain under forest cover**, reflecting a commitment to protecting nature for future generations. 🌿 The contrast raises an important question: **Can urban development truly be called progress if it comes at the cost of the environment?** As Mumbai continues to expand, the debate surrounding Nana Nani Park highlights a larger challenge facing Indian cities: balancing infrastructure development with environmental protection, climate resilience and public well-being. Urban parks and green spaces are not luxuries. They are essential to cleaner air, healthier communities, biodiversity and a better quality of life. A city can build taller skyscrapers and bigger infrastructure projects, but if its residents lose access to nature, what kind of future is it really creating? **Mumbai's 184 trees are more than just a local environmental issue. They represent a larger conversation about sustainable cities, urban development and the true meaning of progress.** What should come first: rapid urban development or protecting the green spaces that make our cities liveable? **Tell us what you think in the comments.** 🌱 #NanaNaniPark #SaveMumbaiTrees #MumbaiNews #Versova #SaveTrees #Bhutan #EarthshotPrize #SustainableDevelopment #ClimateAction #UrbanGreenSpaces #EnvironmentalConservation #MumbaiEnvironment #GreenCities #ClimateChange #thebetterindia [Mumbai Nana Nani Park, Nana Nani Park Versova, 184 trees Mumbai, Mumbai tree cutting controversy, save Mumbai trees, Versova Nana Nani Park, Mumbai environmental news, Bhutan Earthshot Prize, Earthshot Prize 2026, Bhutan forest conservation, Bhutan 60 percent forest cover, sustainable urban development India, Mumbai green spaces, urban deforestation India, environmental conservation India, climate action India, Mumbai development projects, save trees Mumbai, sustainable cities India, urban green spaces importance, The Better India] “Episode” licensed via Music Vine: FWECZ62E8KJQL3BZ Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

items.descriptionOriginal: On the night of 26 November 2008, Mumbai Police officer Sanjay Govilkar was shot while helping capture terrorist Ajmal Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. Across Mumbai, terrorists were attacking several locations. People across India followed the news from their homes, fearful of what might happen next. Police officers responded across the city, and many lost their lives in the process. Sanjay survived the bullet injury. Years later, he continues to speak about that night, the colleagues he lost, and the work that has filled his life beyond the police force. From writing books to helping families through an NGO he founded with friends, he has found different ways to serve people. The Better India spoke to the former officer about the arrest of Kasab and the experiences that shaped his life afterwards. 'Unfortunately, he never returned' "I consider myself very lucky, as the bullet Kasab fired at me hit the left-hand side of my abdomen and not the right," he smiles. Around the time of the attacks, Sanjay had been excited about the release of his book, Stopwatch . He was going around his colleagues' desks to distribute copies to everyone. Shortly before the attacks began in Mumbai, he visited his boss Hemant Karkare's cabin to give him a copy. "Hemant sir was not there for some reason, so I left a copy for him on his desk. Unfortunately, he never returned," Sanjay recalls. The night he helped capture Kasab alive "As the attack unfolded, we were tense, but we had only one goal: to serve our nation. The moment I heard that my boss, Hemant sir, had been attacked and lost his life, I was upset," he shares. Later that night, Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. "My colleague wanted to immediately shoot him down, but I convinced him to arrest him, as he was a key witness," Sanjay shares. Capturing Kasab alive became an important part of the investigation and trial that followed. Sanjay and his fellow police officers confronted Kasab at Girgaum Chowpatty. During the encounter, Sanjay was shot. "After the arrest, I was immediately rushed to the hospital, where I received treatment for five to six days. I was asked to stay away from the news and was given counselling by a group of doctors. Finally, when I was discharged, I saw that all the noise was settling. My doctors and my family took great care of me," he smiles. The experience left Sanjay with a sense of pride in his service, though he is careful to share the credit with his colleagues. When asked how it feels to have achieved something so significant, he says, "I am extremely proud of serving my country, and I would never want to take advantage of this." He goes on to credit his entire team for the recognition. Why a police officer began writing about health While Sanjay says that being a cop and serving the country was his duty, he was always driven by another passion away from work: writing. Sanjay has so far written and published five books, all of them on health, mental health and relationships. One of those was Stopwatch , the book he had just published when the 26/11 attacks took place. "At one point in my career, I was posted as an immigration officer at the airport and had erratic shifts. This took a toll on my health and prompted me to write the book Stopwatch . It is a must-read for all people who work night shifts," he shares. "I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing," he says. Sanjay maintains clear boundaries between his profession and passion. "I never let my professional experiences shape my writing. I incorporate the lessons I have learnt, but never let them influence my writing," he says. 'My biggest asset is my close friends' His friendships have also shaped another important part of his life. Together with his close friends, Sanjay runs Jeevarang, an NGO inspired by a deeply personal experience. "Twenty-five years ago, I lost my grandmother. She was very dear to me. We cremated her in my village, and the next day, when we visited the site to collect her ashes, we saw dogs feeding on the remains. I was heartbroken by what I saw," he shares. The memory stayed with him and became one of the reasons he wanted to help families give their loved ones a dignified farewell. Through Jeevarang, Sanjay and his friends assist families who have lost their loved ones across 21 villages in Maharashtra. They provide support in cash or kind, depending on what the families need. The NGO began operations in 2007 and also encourages writers by sponsoring the publication of their books. A fraud case that inspired his next chapter Sanjay retired from the police in July 2026. But his interest in helping people facing difficult situations has continued into his retirement. He now runs his own legal and risk advisory firm. The idea goes back to a case he encountered during his police career, involving a mother and daughter who lost their livelihood to online fraud. "I came across a peculiar case in my career in 2009. Online fraudsters tricked a mother and daughter. They were told they had won a lottery and were asked to pay a huge sum of money. The women were innocent and, assuming they would receive a large amount, they sold their small pull-cart shop in Mumbai and lost all their money. The department, however, intervened and cracked the case. This incident stayed with me, and I decided that I wanted to help people who feel stuck in legal issues. That's when I came up with this idea," he shares. The mother and daughter's experience stayed with Sanjay, much like what he had witnessed after his grandmother's cremation years earlier. Both experiences influenced the work he eventually chose to pursue outside policing. When Sanjay speaks about 26/11, he credits his colleagues for what they achieved together. In the years since, he has continued to act on the concerns that have stayed with him, from helping families arrange a dignified farewell to supporting people facing legal difficulties. Individuals seeking guidance or assistance with legal matters and risk-related concerns can find information about the services offered by Govilkar Legal & Risk Advisory on its official website . The firm aims to help people understand complex legal situations and consider their next steps.

items.descriptionOriginal: You twist open a sealed bottle of water and drink without a second thought. It's clear, it's sealed, and it's been purified. Behind that bottle is more checking than most of us realise. Since November 2024, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has treated packaged drinking water as a "high-risk" food. The label doesn't mean the water is dangerous. It means the product gets stricter scrutiny: inspections before a licence is granted, annual inspections, and regular testing of both the water and its packaging. Those checks exist because some things in water can't be seen, smelt or tasted. A recent case shows why they matter. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. The sample reportedly contained bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, above the limit of 10. A referral laboratory later also found polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs. Bisleri disputes the findings. It says independent testing found bromate within the limit, that its water is safe, and that it will cooperate with the regulator. Whatever the outcome, the case raises a question most of us have never thought to ask: if water has been purified, how can chemicals linked to cancer end up in it? Here's what bromate and PAHs are, how they get into water, what levels are considered acceptable, and what the rules say about keeping them out. What happened at Bisleri's Goa plant? On 30 September 2025, FSSAI officials collected six samples from Bisleri's Goa facility. According to the company, five met the standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre, two above the limit. FSSAI has sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International Pvt Ltd after a water sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Photograph: (Plastic Pollution Coalition) Bisleri says it appealed on 22 November 2025, and the sample went to a referral laboratory. That lab found bromate within the limit, but detected PAHs. Bisleri also had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved lab, which it says found bromate within the permitted limit. It sent those results to FSSAI's Western Regional Office on 2 February 2026 . After that, the company says, it heard nothing more and assumed the matter was closed. FSSAI, however, declared the sample unsafe and sanctioned prosecution under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. It has also said it plans to test more samples from Bisleri and other packaged water companies. A prosecution sanction is not a conviction. And because the labs reported different results, it matters to separate what each test actually found from what is still disputed. How does bromate get into water? Surprisingly, bromate often comes from the very step meant to make water safe. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. But some water sources naturally contain bromide. When ozone meets bromide during treatment, the reaction can produce bromate. The World Health Organization (WHO) says this treatment process, called ozonation , is the main reason bromate shows up in drinking water. Normally, it isn't found in water in any significant amount. How much forms depends on four things: how much bromide was in the water to begin with how much ozone is used the water's pH (how acidic or alkaline it is) how long treatment runs Get the balance wrong and levels can climb. The WHO has recorded bromate anywhere from under 2 to 293 micrograms per litre in ozone-treated water. Many bottlers disinfect water with ozone, a powerful gas that kills bacteria and viruses. Photograph: (The Hospital of Central Connecticut) Bromate can also form when chlorine-based disinfectants are produced using salt that contains bromide impurities. So bromate in water doesn't necessarily mean the source was polluted. It can be a by-product of cleaning the water, which is why the treatment process itself needs close watching. How much is too much? Bromate worries scientists because it caused cancer in laboratory animals. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Its 1999 review found strong evidence of cancer in animals, but not enough evidence in humans. That difference matters. A chemical being a possible cancer hazard doesn't mean every exposure carries the same risk. How much is present, and for how long someone is exposed, both count. The WHO's provisional limit for bromate in drinking water is 10 micrograms per litre (0.01 milligrams per litre). India's standard for packaged drinking water, BIS IS 14543:2024, also lists bromate as a chemical that must be tested. In the Bisleri case, 12 micrograms is two above the limit. That's a regulatory concern, but it doesn't mean anyone who drank the water will develop cancer or fall ill. Judging the real risk would need three things: how concentrated it was, how much someone drank, and for how long. Two things are true at once. Detecting a chemical doesn't automatically make water unsafe, because it's the amount that counts. And staying within the limit doesn't mean manufacturers can stop checking. What are PAHs, and how do they get into water? PAHs are a large family of chemicals, built from two or more linked rings of carbon atoms. They form mainly when things don't burn completely, such as coal, wood, petrol and other organic material. Vehicle exhaust, factory emissions and other burning release them into the air and the environment. PAHs don't dissolve easily in water. Instead, they tend to cling to tiny particles. According to the WHO , one known route into drinking water is the coal-tar coating used inside older water pipes to stop them corroding. Pollution from burning can also settle on soil and water, and wash into water sources as runoff. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies potassium bromate as Group 2B, or "possibly carcinogenic to humans". Photograph: (Image generated by AI) One PAH, benzo[a]pyrene, is a particular concern because it can cause cancer. The WHO's limit for it is 0.7 micrograms per litre. But PAHs are not all alike. One compound causing cancer doesn't mean they all carry the same risk. Finding PAHs in a sample also doesn't tell us how they got there. In the Bisleri case, we would need to know which compounds were found, and in what amounts, to judge how serious the finding is or where it came from. What about the plastic bottle? Bromate comes mainly from treatment, not the bottle. But scientists have looked at whether chemicals can leach from packaging into water. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. It found that the amount of plasticisers seeping into water depended on the packaging material, how long the water was stored and how hot it got. Leaching was higher at high temperatures, especially in recycled PET bottles and plastic packets. That's a good reason to pay attention to packaging and storage. But the study looked at phthalates, not bromate or PAHs, so it doesn't show that bottles caused either contaminant discussed here. What checks are already in place? Under FSSAI's 29 November 2024 order , packaged drinking water is a high-risk food category. This means: manufacturers must be inspected before they get a licence or registration inspections happen once a year centrally licensed manufacturers need an annual third-party food safety audit by an FSSAI-recognised agency From 1 January 2026, a new FSSAI testing scheme also requires manufacturers to: test their source water at FSSAI-notified, NABL-accredited labs before using it, and test any new source before it's used test for microbes every month, and for several chemicals every quarter test every parameter in the standard at least once every six months test monthly if a parameter fails, until three batches in a row pass The packaging is covered too. Bottles, jars and caps must be tested every six months for "overall and colour migration", meaning whether material or colour seeps from the packaging into the water. Manufacturers must keep these records for inspection. How does a failed sample end up in court? The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 , sets out the steps (Sections 42, 46 and 47): A Food Safety Officer collects a sample and sends it to a Food Analyst, who usually has 14 days to report. If the manufacturer disputes the result, it can appeal to the Designated Officer, who can send the sample to a referral laboratory. If the findings show a violation serious enough to prosecute, the case goes to the relevant authority for sanction. A 2022 study in the Bulletin of Environmental Contamination and Toxicology tested PET bottles and low-density polyethylene water packets in India. Photograph: (Food & Wine) In the Bisleri case, the company challenged the first result, the sample went to a referral lab, and FSSAI then sanctioned prosecution. Bisleri's independent results and its response are part of a dispute that will now be settled through the regulatory and legal process. Should consumers be worried? Chemical contaminants can't always be detected by taste, smell or look. Clear water isn't necessarily free of chemicals . But the Bisleri findings concern one regulatory sample. They don't prove that all packaged water, or every batch from the company, is unsafe. Safe drinking water depends on consistent testing and monitoring. Purification is non-negotiable, but the chemicals that can form during treatment, and contamination from storage and pipes, deserve just as much attention.

items.descriptionOriginal: When trees along a road are marked for felling, the loss extends beyond their shade and canopy. For thousands of orchids growing on their trunks and branches, the removal of a single tree can mean losing their entire habitat. In Kozhikode, Kerala, researchers faced this challenge as road-widening projects threatened mature trees supporting native orchids. Instead of allowing the plants to be lost along with the trees, they began rescuing and relocating them to other landscapes. A study published on 15 October 2026 in the scientific journal Plants has now documented the outcomes of this effort. Researchers assessed 27,324 native orchids belonging to 21 species that were relocated to three sites in Kozhikode. After monitoring them for 12 to 24 months, they found that 19,511, or 71.4%, had survived. Why roadside trees matter to orchids Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. They use trees as support, relying on their bark, moisture, shade and surrounding canopy conditions to survive. When a mature host tree is felled, the orchids growing on it can lose their habitat at once. The scale of this dependence is evident from an earlier survey in Kerala. A 2025 study, Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot , recorded nearly 10,000 orchids belonging to 13 species on approximately 600 trees across Wayanad. The trees represented 72 different taxa, and the orchid population included six regional endemics. The October 2026 study notes that road construction and widening have increasingly threatened these mature host trees and the orchid communities they support. The researchers involved in the latest study included Mithun Venugopal and Pradeep N Sukumaran of the KSCSTE-Malabar Botanical Garden and Institute for Plant Sciences in Kozhikode, and Viswambharan Sarasan of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, in the UK. More than 17,000 native orchids representing 22 species had initially been transferred to Sarovaram Biopark as part of the earlier rescue programme. The subsequent effort also involved relocating orchids to two other sites: the Malabar Botanical Garden and Kappad Beach. Three sites, different survival outcomes The researchers examined how the rescued plants adapted to three distinct environments, all located in Kozhikode's coastal region. Sarovaram Biopark, an urban wetland with mangrove cover, provided a humid and relatively sheltered environment. The Malabar Botanical Garden offered a mix of shaded, marshy and moderately elevated areas. Unlike terrestrial orchids that grow in soil, epiphytic orchids grow on the trunks and branches of other plants. Photograph: (tspkumar via iNaturalist) Kappad Beach, meanwhile, exposed the orchids to stronger winds, direct sunlight and salt spray. The differences were reflected in their survival. According to the study, Sarovaram recorded the strongest overall establishment , while the exposed coastal location presented greater challenges for the plants to take root and survive. However, Kappad recorded the highest flowering rate among surviving orchids, at 35.6%. It also had the highest proportion of flowering plants producing capsules, at 62.3%. At Sarovaram, the corresponding figures were 26.3% and 34.8%, while the Malabar Botanical Garden recorded 27% and 40.1%, respectively. What the findings mean for conservation The study also examined 6,126 rescued orchids belonging to 12 regionally endemic species. Of these, 3,368 survived, translating to a survival rate of 55%. The group included eight species endemic to India and four shared between southern India and Sri Lanka. This was lower than the overall survival rate of 71.4%, highlighting the additional challenges involved in relocating species with more restricted natural distributions. The researchers found that some high-altitude and mist-forest-associated orchids also managed to survive and reproduce after being moved to lower elevations, although their establishment depended more on the receiving site. Orchids of India Calanthe biloba Lindl. #Orchids #India #Conservation #Biodiversity @ForestDeptt @Sdg13Un https://t.co/mZDyHDj2Mc — Dr. Sanjeet Kumar (Ecologist) (@BiotechSanjeet) October 19, 2026 Beyond survival, the researchers also looked at whether the rescued orchids could reproduce in their new surroundings. They found capsules containing embryos among the relocated plants , indicating that some had progressed beyond simply adapting to their new locations. However, the team stresses that relocation is not a substitute for protecting natural habitats. It is an additional conservation measure for situations where the removal of orchid-bearing trees cannot be avoided. Before a tree is marked for felling to make way for a wider road, there may be dozens of plants growing quietly on its trunk and branches. For orchids, the loss of that tree can mean the loss of an entire habitat. Identifying these plants before construction begins can make room for infrastructure without overlooking the smaller ecosystems that depend on the trees being removed. Sources: 'When Roads Remove Trees, Conservation Must Move Fast: A Rescue Translocation Model for Keralam's Native Epiphytic Orchids' : By Mithun Venugopal , Pradeep N. Sukumaran, Viswambharan Sarasan, Published on 15 October 2026 'Distribution and Abundance of Native Orchids on Roadside Trees in a Global Biodiversity Hotspot' : By Viswambharan Sarasan, Mithun Venugopal, Ratheesh M. Η διαδικασία, που ονομάζεται Totally Endosco…
items.descriptionOriginal: #thebetterindia What if surgeons could perform a heart bypass without stopping the heart? Two Indian doctors just made it possible! At Medanta Hospital in Gurugram, Dr Nitin Kumar Rajput and Dr Lalit Malik performed a complex heart bypass using five robotic arms controlled through two separate surgeon consoles. The procedure, called Totally Endoscopic Coronary Artery Bypass (TECAB), was performed through tiny incisions without the conventional large chest incision or stopping the heart. A specialised stabiliser held the area being operated on steady while the heart continued beating. No heart-lung machine was needed. This was the world’s first reported dual-console, five-arm robotic beating-heart TECAB procedure. And here’s another reason to celebrate: the robot used was SSi Mantra, developed in India by SS Innovations, founded by cardiac surgeon Dr Sudhir Srivastava. The patient’s recovery has been encouraging. A remarkable step forward for Indian medical innovation and the future of minimally invasive heart surgery! #RoboticSurgery #HeartSurgery #MedicalInnovation #MakeInIndia #IndianInnovation [Robotic heart bypass surgery in India, world’s first beating-heart TECAB, SSi Mantra surgical robot, Indian-mad Subscribe Us Now : https://www.youtube.com/thebetterindia Follow us for more: Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/thebetterindia Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/thebetterindia/ Twitter: https://twitter.com/thebetterindia LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/thebetterindia/ Website: https://www.thebetterindia.com/

Για χρόνια, το θέαμα μιας ενυδρίδας που κολυμπά…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of The Better India's new wildlife series, Species in Focus: 52 species. 52 stories. 52 reasons to protect India's wildlife. One species at a time, the series explores India's rare, endangered and lesser-known wildlife, their habitats, behaviour, ecological roles and conservation status. For years, the sight of an otter swimming through Kashmir's rivers had become rare. Once found across the Jhelum River basin, the Eurasian otter (Lutra lutra) had nearly disappeared from the valley, its numbers declining amid fur-driven poaching, habitat destruction and water pollution. Now, after decades of little evidence of its presence, the elusive mammal is being spotted again in Kashmir's waterways. A study published in the journal Biological Diversity on 23 October 2026, titled Re-Emergence of Eurasian Otter (Lutra lutra) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge , documents recent sightings and field evidence of the species in the valley. Authored by Irfan Khursheed Shah and Sohail Ahmad Wagay, the study brings together reports that suggest the otter is reappearing after decades of near-local extinction. The researchers identify historical hunting for fur, habitat destruction, and water pollution as major reasons behind the species' decline. Srinagar had once served as a commercial centre for the valley's pelt and fur trade. Although wildlife protection measures introduced from the late 1970s onwards helped curb hunting and the trade, the otter population had already fallen sharply. The return was first noticed in 2025 According to the October 2026 paper, the first widely reported public evidence of the otter's return emerged in June 2025, when a video of an animal in a tributary of the Lidder River went viral. Viewers initially mistook it for a crocodile. The researchers say that professional enhancement of the footage helped establish that the animal was a Eurasian otter, a species that had become unfamiliar to many residents. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Photograph: (IUCN Otter Specialist Group Bulletin) Following the video, camera traps were installed along the Rambiara and Lidder tributaries in July 2025. Although these did not capture the animals, researchers photographed spraints (otter droppings), which can help establish an animal's presence in an area. Another video subsequently surfaced from Ganderbal district, showing an otter feeding on a fish in the Sindh stream, another tributary of the Jhelum. Together, these records provided evidence of the animal's presence across different parts of the valley . The findings also build on earlier field research. A separate study published in the IUCN/SSC Otter Specialist Group Bulletin in January 2026 documented Eurasian otters in the Hirpora Wildlife Sanctuary, along the Rambiara River catchment in Shopian district. The Wildlife Trust of India researchers Tanushree Srivastava, Manvi Singh, Muneeb Nazir and Ishwar Narayanan, along with Sohail Ahmad Wagay of the J&K Department of Wildlife Protection, recorded an initial direct sighting during fieldwork in March 2024. They subsequently conducted a systematic survey between April and June 2025, covering a 12-km stretch of the river. The team recorded 21 signs of otter presence, including one direct sighting, spraints, pugmarks, tracks, fish-feeding remains, and camera-trap photographs. The study reported an average encounter rate of 0.34 signs per kilometre and a camera-trap capture rate of 4.31 captures per 100 trap nights. However, neither study establishes the total number of otters now living in Kashmir Valley. Why the return matters for freshwater ecosystems The Eurasian otter is classified as Near Threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List. It is a semi-aquatic mammal that inhabits rivers, streams, and other freshwater environments. As a top predator, it helps regulate prey populations and is considered an indicator of freshwater ecosystem health. A separate finding from the Hirpora study also points to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Only 15% of respondents recognised the Eurasian otter, although 92% supported its conservation. More than half reported declining fish populations in the area, indicating potential ecological pressures that also affect otter habitats. What could threaten their return? The October study cautions that the conditions in Kashmir's waterways have changed considerably since the period when otters were commonly reported. Urban expansion over paddy fields, conversion of agricultural land into apple orchards and construction along riverbanks have reduced and fragmented potential habitats. The decline in traditional irrigation canals has further affected the network of waterways available to the animals. The researchers also identify river pollution from heavy metals, pesticides, microplastics, and plastic waste as potential threats. Destructive fishing practices involving chemicals and electric currents, human disturbance and the increasing presence of stray dogs could further affect their survival. We are into the middle stage of our '13 Weeks of Otters' series, and next up we have one that the IOSF are very familiar with, the Eurasian Otter! Photo by Terry Evans! #Conservation #Eurasian #Otter #Wild https://t.co/NBY5RQ0ZNR https://t.co/CklFyxizXv — International Otter Survival Fund (IOSF) (@IOSF) August 8, 2022 Climate change presents another challenge. Changes in water levels, floods, landslides and prolonged dry spells can damage or expose the sheltered riverbank spaces, known as holts, where otters rest and raise their young. The researchers also flag the possibility of conflict with expanding trout farms , which are an increasingly important source of livelihood in the valley. What conservation efforts need to focus on The October 2026 paper recommends a coordinated conservation plan involving researchers, wildlife authorities and conservation organisations. This includes protecting and improving river habitats, addressing pollution, preventing hunting and monitoring the species across its newly documented locations. It also calls for public awareness campaigns to address misconceptions about otters. The researchers recommend educational initiatives in schools, awareness material in local languages and outreach at tourist destinations to help residents recognise the species and understand its behaviour. The authors note that otter encounters rarely result in harm to humans globally, and that most interactions are neutral. Better public understanding, therefore, is an important part of ensuring the animals can persist in waterways shared with people. For now, the recent records establish the Eurasian otter's presence in Kashmir's river systems, rather than a confirmed recovery of its population. Sustained monitoring and protection of these freshwater habitats will be necessary to determine whether the species can establish a lasting presence in the valley. Sources: 'Re‐Emergence of Eurasian Otter ( Lutra Lutra ) in the Valley of Kashmir, India: A Conservation Triumph and a Challenge' : By Irfan Khursheed Shah, Sohail Ahmad Wagay, Published in October 2026 'Eurasian Otters Make Remarkable Re-Emergence In Kashmir Valley After Decades-Long Absence' : By Eurasia Review, Published on 8 November 2026 'An Overview on Lutra lutra' : By Seyed Parsa Mousavi, Mohammad Mahdi Ramzanipour, and Mohammad Forouhar Vajargah, Published on 15 April 2023 'The Satpura Otter Saga' : By Raza Kazmi, Wildlife Conservation Trust, Published in December 2024

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Baby Elephant Rescue Zuri Thrives Months After Septic Tank Ordeal Reading Time: 3 minutes Baby elephant rescue Zuri has thrived for months at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s Nairobi Nursery after nearly drowning in a septic tank in Kenya. Baby elephant rescue stories rarely end as well as Zuri’s. Found trapped inside a septic tank near Voi Safari Lodge in Kenya when she was just days old, the calf has spent the past months recovering at the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust’s nursery in Nairobi. Keepers now describe a confident, food-driven toddler who has already claimed the role of herd princess. Rescuers worked late into the night to free Zuri from the tank, a traumatic ordeal for any elephant calf, let alone one only days old. After a night of stabilization at the Trust’s nearby Voi facility, she was flown to the Nairobi Nursery for round-the-clock care. The Nairobi Nursery is the first stop in a rehabilitation journey that can stretch for more than a decade. Orphaned elephants typically arrive after losing their mothers to poaching, drought, conflict, or accidents like Zuri’s. Keepers assign each calf a dedicated human caregiver who stays close around the clock, standing in for the mother an orphan has lost. Each baby elephant rescue brings its own logistical demands. Calves depend on a specialized milk formula that took decades of trial and error to perfect, since cow’s milk alone proved fatal to earlier generations of rescued elephants. Round-the-clock bottle feeding, veterinary monitoring, and a rotating team of keepers all continue for months or years after a calf first arrives. Within days of arriving, Zuri settled into the nursery herd and quickly displaced an older calf as the group’s most doted-on member. Several older orphans now compete to shepherd her around, with one in particular walking her into her stable each evening for weeks, until Zuri felt ready to go in alone. Keepers describe Zuri as anything but timid. She reportedly bangs on her stable door the moment she hears a wheelbarrow of milk bottles approaching at night, and sprints toward keepers with her trunk raised during the day, visibly displeased if a bottle isn’t ready and waiting. She has even tried stealing bottles from an older herd mate after finishing her own. Despite her boldness, Zuri shows a softer side around the nursery’s newest arrival, a recently rescued calf not yet publicly introduced. Keepers say Zuri doesn’t treat the newcomer as a rival the way she does with some of the older toddlers, a distinction they see as a promising sign of her continued emotional development. Bold enough to bang on her stable door at feeding time and steal milk bottles from herd mates, Zuri also shows a gentler side with the nursery’s newest arrival, a sign keepers read as promising emotional growth in the baby elephant rescue. Photo courtesy of Sheldrick Wildlife Trust . Not every trace of the ordeal has faded. Zuri remains wary of unfamiliar people and some of her own keepers, a caution the Trust attributes to her brush with drowning and the fear she experienced during the traumatic rescue. Recovery from early trauma varies widely between individual elephants, and keepers say patience, gentle care, reassurance, and close observation, rather than a fixed timeline, guide each calf’s progress. Over time, they hope Zuri will continue building confidence and feel increasingly secure in her new environment. Zuri’s progress reflects decades of institutional experience behind this kind of baby elephant rescue work. The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust has run its elephant rescue and rehabilitation program since the 1970s, hand-raising hundreds of orphans and successfully returning most to wild herds in Tsavo. Public support directly funds this kind of work. Individual donors can foster a specific orphan, supporting a program that covers keeper salaries, milk formula, and veterinary costs for calves like Zuri. That funding model has let the Trust scale its operations even as new rescue calls keep coming in from across Kenya. Around three years old, Zuri will eventually graduate from the nursery to one of the Trust’s reintegration units in Tsavo, following the same path generations of orphans before her took. For now, her days are filled with milk, mischief, and the attention of a devoted entourage of nannies. For a calf whose baby elephant rescue began three months ago with a near-drowning in a septic tank, that counts as a very good life. items.descriptionOriginal: Your weight is going up. Your sleep isn’t great either. Can poor sleep really affect weight? Yes, it can, and weight can affect sleep too. One bad night isn’t the story. It’s the repeated pattern that matters. Repeated sleep loss can make hunger harder to manage, food choices harder to get right, and even planning or staying active feel more difficult. There is a bigger picture too. Snoring alone doesn’t mean you have a sleep disorder. But loud, habitual snoring, gasping during sleep, or someone noticing that you stop breathing, along with persistent daytime sleepiness, are reasons to speak to a doctor. So protect your regular sleep, have balanced meals, keep moving and include strength activity where appropriate. And speak to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs as well as whether a sleep assessment is right for you. Treating weight as part of the health picture is responsible medical care. Not shameful. Not cheating. Not failure. Not a shortcut. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #SleepHealth #WeightManagement #SleepAndWeight #HealthyHabits [sleep and weight gain, can poor sleep cause weight gain, snoring and sleep assessment, weight and sleep problems, India]
