items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Rangers Gain New Tools for Protecting Whale Sharks in the Maldives Reading Time: 3 minutes Rangers protecting whale sharks in the Maldives now have new tools to help manage heavy tourism and boat traffic in the South Ari Marine Protected Area. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has a new set of tools. In August 2026, rangers at the South Ari Marine Protected Area (SAMPA) received new equipment. Thermal cameras, body cameras, and a vessel-tracking device now help them enforce rules in busy waters. Tech4Nature , a partnership between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and Huawei, provided the tools. The program, part of Huawei’s Tech4All initiative, helps protected areas use technology to meet global management standards. Designated in 2009, South Ari is the Maldives’ largest marine protected area. It covers about 5,600 hectares, nearly the size of Manhattan. Whale sharks gather there all year, making it a site of global importance for the species. Researchers have identified more than 910 whale sharks in the Maldives since 2006, mostly in South Ari. Most are young males that use the area to feed and grow. Whale sharks are the largest fish in the ocean and are listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List. These sharks draw more than 65,000 visitors a year, or about 180 every day. A 2014 study valued South Ari’s whale shark tourism at USD 9.4 million in 2013 alone. The same boats that bring that income also pose a serious threat. Whale sharks feed on plankton near the surface, where visitors can easily see them. That same habit puts them in the path of passing boats. A 2021 study in Scientific Reports found that 61% of South Ari’s whale sharks suffered major boat-strike injuries. Injured sharks tended to stay in the area longer, likely to heal in warm, food-rich water. However, staying put may mean fewer trips to breeding grounds. The researchers also pointed to a gap in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. At the time, the area’s boating rules were suggestions, with little enforcement. SAMPA ranger Ali Gasim lists speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution among the main problems. Speeding boats are the same risk the 2021 study linked to injuries. With limited resources, his team struggles to monitor such a large stretch of ocean. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives remains difficult because boating rules in the area were once only suggestions with little enforcement, and SAMPA rangers, working with limited resources, struggle to monitor a large stretch of ocean while speeding vessels, crowding, and light pollution persist. Photo by Derek Keats on Pexels. Tech4Nature began by measuring those gaps. In April 2026, the team ran a baseline review with the IUCN Green List Self-Assessment Tool. The IUCN Green List is a global standard for well-managed protected areas. That review confirmed two needs: more operational capacity and stronger day-to-day enforcement. Each piece of new equipment was chosen to meet them. A vessel-mounted thermal camera detects heat, so rangers can spot boats after dark. A vessel tracking device helps them follow boat movements across the protected area. Together, these tools extend patrols into hours and places that were hard to watch before. Body cameras let rangers record encounters and collect evidence of violations. A telephoto lens lets rangers document sharks and vessels from a distance. Clear records make it much easier to take action against boats that speed or crowd an animal. Rangers completed introductory training and field tests in August 2026. The sessions covered camera use and maintenance, and how to fit the tools into existing patrol routines. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives also depends on partners who can act on rangers’ records. The project works with the Maldives Ministry of Climate Change, Environment and Energy and the Maldives Police Service. Maldives Whale Shark Research and the Big Fish Network also contribute. Founded in 2013, Maldives Whale Shark Research tracks individual sharks over time. Each whale shark has a unique pattern of spots behind its gills that photos can identify. Divers and tourists can add their own photos to Wildbook for Whale Sharks, a global online database. That long-term record is key to measuring progress in protecting whale sharks in the Maldives. It can show whether new injuries become less common as enforcement improves. Muhusina Abdul Rahman, director of the Protected Areas Section, says innovation is essential where marine park resources are limited. Najfa Shaheem Razee, who manages the Maldives Country Program, says the project links real management needs with targeted support. The project will continue to support monitoring and data collection in South Ari. The 2014 economic study had already called for licensed operators, a code of conduct, and GPS logbooks for boats. The new tools bring several of those ideas within reach. Protecting whale sharks in the Maldives has always meant managing boats and people, not just sharks. With better tools , a small ranger team can now see more and act faster. If injuries fall, South Ari could become a model for other whale shark sites. The post Rangers Gain New Tools for Protecting Whale Sharks in the Maldives appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The best holiday parties tend to be the ones where nobody thinks about the hosting at all. Guests walk in, find a spot for their coat, settle in with a plate and a drink, and the evening carries them along. When something’s slightly off, though, they feel it long before they’d ever say it out loud. A guest who can’t hear the person next to them, or who’s stuck eating bread rolls all night because everything else has nuts in it, probably won’t complain. They’ll just leave a little earlier than they planned. The good news is that most of these little snags are easy to catch if you picture the evening from your guests’ side of the door. So let’s walk through it the way they will, from the moment they pull up to the moment they say goodbye. Before holiday guests arrive A clean home where it counts First impressions start at the entryway. Clutter underfoot or a sink full of dishes can make guests more focused on where to step than on catching up with each other. You don’t need a spotless house, though. Rooms that will stay closed can wait. Put your energy into the spaces people will use, like the bathroom, kitchen, and living room, plus the guest room if anyone’s staying over. Spreading the cleaning across a few days instead of saving it all for the night before keeps you from running on fumes when the doorbell rings. Parking, coats and the weather Even a beautifully decorated party can feel disorganized if guests circle the block looking for a parking spot or end up holding their coats for the first half hour. A short message a few days ahead covering where to park and what to expect when they arrive takes the guesswork out of it. If you live somewhere with snow or ice, it helps to have a backup plan ready in case the weather turns on the day. Food everyone can eat Nobody wants to be the guest pushing food around a plate because of an allergy the host didn’t know about. Before you settle on a menu, send a quick note asking whether anyone has dietary needs. Even if no one replies with anything, having a few dishes that happen to be gluten-free, vegan, or nut-free is an easy way to make sure no one goes hungry. Making holiday guests comfortable once the party starts Room to move around Every home has its own quirks, and the layout shapes how comfortable people feel once they’re inside. Before the party, take a slow lap through your space as if you’d never seen it. Where will people gather? Is the buffet in a spot that blocks the hallway? Is there somewhere to sit near the food? Shumaila Panhwar , a hosting professional, recommends exactly that kind of walkthrough. “When you walk through the space from the perspective of the guests and their experience, it makes it easier to determine placement of items and what makes sense best for flow,” she advises. Music that stays in the background A festive playlist does wonders for the mood, right up until people have to lean in and shout to hear each other. Keep the volume low enough that conversation comes first. Your neighbors will appreciate it too, and nothing ends a party faster than a noise complaint. Being a present host Let yourself enjoy it Here’s the one that catches even the most organized hosts. It’s easy to spend the whole evening refilling bowls and checking the oven, but your guests came to see you. Your presence matters most when people are meeting for the first time and could use an introduction to get a conversation going. Making a plan the night before and running through it once can help a lot. When you know everything is ready, it gets easier to set down the serving spoon, pour yourself a glass of something, and join the people you invited, which, when you think about it, is what made you want to host in the first place. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post 6 hosting habits that leave holiday guests feeling uneasy (and how to avoid them) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A cell therapy built to fight cancer is helping people with stiff person syndrome get back on their feet. In an early trial led by neurologists at Mayo Clinic, patients who had needed family members to help them walk and handle daily tasks regained enough function to return to work, exercise, and hobbies after a single round of CAR-T cell therapy. The results, published in JAMA Neurology , point to a treatment that targets the root of the disease instead of only easing its symptoms. A rare disease with no cure What stiff person syndrome does to the body Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the central nervous system. The result can be severe rigidity throughout the body, painful muscle spasms, and frequent falls. Decades of research have produced treatments that can soften symptoms, but none that cure it. The condition drew global attention in December 2022, when singer Céline Dion revealed her diagnosis . In an Instagram video, she said it affected “every aspect of my daily life,” including her ability to sing. How CAR-T works against stiff person syndrome CAR-T therapy is already an established treatment for some blood cancers. Doctors extract a patient’s T cells, a type of immune cell, and engineer them in a lab to seek out and destroy specific targets. For this trial, the cells were redesigned to eliminate the immune cells that drive SPS, using a CD19-targeted therapy called mivocabtagene autoleucel. Each participant received a single treatment, and the study ran across three sites, Mayo Clinic among them. Dr. Anastasia Zekeridou , a neurologist and researcher at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, said the scale of the response stood out. “What was most striking was the degree of improvement we saw in some patients,” she said. “With existing treatments, we may be able to improve symptoms but we very rarely see patients return to their previous level of function.” Patients back at work and on the treadmill Jonathan Walden: hunting and fishing again Before the trial, Jonathan Walden relied on his family for help with walking and basic daily tasks. He has since returned to his job. “I can go to work every single day. I can do everything I did before. I go hunting; I can go fishing,” he said. “I have not had one episode since receiving treatment.” Shari St. Germain: seven minutes on a treadmill Shari St. Germain’s illness progressed from severe leg cramps and trouble walking to rigid muscles and falls. After CAR-T, she said, each day has felt “better and better.” One morning she felt well enough to try the treadmill. “My husband comes running in because I’m crying and he’s like: ‘Are you OK?’ And I’m like: ‘I just walked for seven minutes on the treadmill,'” she said. Next questions for CAR-T in neurology Will the improvements last? The researchers are clear that this is early evidence from a small, nonrandomized trial, and that larger studies are needed. “These early results are very encouraging and the key question now is whether those improvements will be sustained over time,” Zekeridou said. Beyond blood cancer Dr. Sean Pittock, who chairs the department of neurology at Mayo Clinic, sees a wider opening. “CAR-T therapy has already transformed the treatment of some cancers, and we are now beginning to see its potential in autoimmune neurologic diseases,” he said, adding that the results offer hope for other immune-mediated neurologic conditions with few effective options. Yasmin Sheikh, head of policy and public affairs at the UK blood cancer charity Anthony Nolan, which was not involved in the trial, called the research “an exciting development” and more evidence that CAR-T could reach well beyond blood cancer. If the gains hold in larger trials, people with stiff person syndrome could have something they have never had before: a treatment aimed at giving them back the lives the disease took, not just making those lives easier to manage. items.descriptionOriginal: Scientists have long used chemogenetics to study brains in the lab. A pilot trial for seizures is its first leap into medicine. Flashing lights. Buzzing noises. A sudden wave of fear. For some people with epilepsy, these sensations herald an oncoming seizure. Drugs can keep some seizures at bay, but over 30 percent of patients don’t respond to them, a statistic that hasn’t budged in decades. Frequent, uncontrolled seizures rob people of a normal life. They can’t drive or swim alone. Some struggle to stay in school, hold down jobs, or maintain relationships. And despite growing public awareness, stigma lingers. For people with severe drug-resistant epilepsy, surgery is an option. If the seizures are associated with a local brain region, doctors can remove the tissue. It’s a drastic operation, but it isn’t rare. In 2024, over 2,000 patients elected to undergo the procedure. Depending on the brain region removed, surgery can control seizures in nearly 70 percent of patients, but they risk losing memory, language, and other cognitive abilities. A new gene therapy could offer an alternative. In a clinical trial , three men who had lived with epilepsy for at least a decade saw monthly seizures drop over 90 percent. One remained seizure-free for a year. In the trial, the team shuttled a gene into a small patch of the hippocampus, the source of their seizures. The gene produces a kind of protein “dimmer switch” in neurons. Normally silent, the protein springs into action when activated by an FDA-approved drug, allowing scientists to dial down the region’s electrical activity rather than shutting it off completely—something that’s not possible with current treatments. The technology, called chemogenetics, has been a staple of animal research in neuroscience. The findings, though early, suggest it could finally make the leap into human medicine. “It certainly has caused a lot of excitement in the field,” said Dimitri Kullmann at University College London to Chemical & Engineering News , who was not involved in the study. Chemical Romance Intricate webs of neurons underlie every brain function. Our ability to feel, move, remember, and reason all stem from electrical and chemical signals that wire brain cells into circuits. It’s a delicate balance. Some neurons release chemicals that fire up their neighbors; others dampen them. In epilepsy, this goes awry. The causes are plenty. Genetic mutations can disrupt how neurons develop or function. Brain injuries, tumors, stroke, and infections can also fuel the condition. In some frustrating cases, the culprit remains unknown. Rebalancing these circuits could tame runaway seizures. Most antiseizure drugs prevent neurons from firing too rapidly or boosting inhibitory chemical signals. But medication is a Band-Aid, not a cure. Because the drugs flood the whole brain, they can trigger fatigue, dizziness, mood swings, and sometimes more serious side effects , including liver or heart problems. Dampening electrical activity at the source could be a better bet. Around two decades ago, an emerging technology called chemogenetics first amazed neuroscientists with its precise control of single neurons. The technology relies on two parts: gene therapy and a drug. First, an engineered virus delivers a gene encoding a designer receptor into targeted neurons. The receptor is silent until a specific drug activates it. By adjusting the drug’s dose, scientists can fine tune the activity of modified neurons. Rather than simply flicking neurons on or off, the approach is flexible and targeted. Chemogenetics soon caught the attention of epilepsy researchers. In 2019, a team at Ghent University in Belgium tested the method in mice with seizures originating in the hippocampus. They delivered a designer receptor called hMADi to the region. A single dose of clozapine, an FDA-approved antipsychotic, controlled seizures for at least 15 hours. With repeated treatment, seizures nearly vanished. A subsequent study in monkeys also dramatically slashed seizures. Given these encouraging findings, some researchers were ready to take the next step. “I think scientists like me felt like, ‘Why haven’t we tried it in humans yet?’” said study author Minmin Luo at the Chinese Institute for Brain Research. Restoring Balance The trial enrolled three men under 40 diagnosed with epilepsy for 10 to 25 years. All had tried at least two antiseizure medications without success. Brain scans traced their seizures to a scarred hippocampus on one side of the brain. The same structure on the other side remained healthy. Despite their long history of epilepsy, none showed notable signs of cognitive troubles. Similar to previous work, the team delivered a gene encoding the hMADi receptor into the damaged region of each patient’s hippocampus in a series of three shots. A dye mixed with the therapy confirmed it reached nearly the entire region in two patients and spread slightly beyond it in the third. The infusion took roughly two hours. Two weeks later, the men began taking clozapine pills every eight hours. After five months, their average monthly seizure count had dropped from roughly four to nearly zero. Brain recordings also showed far fewer epilepsy-related electrical spikes, and their damaged hippocampuses increased metabolism, though levels remained below those in the region’s healthy counterpart. The benefits lasted. In check-ups throughout the following year, two patients remained seizure-free. The third experienced two “breakthrough” seizures after an unexpected interruption in medication, but the seizures stopped once he restarted the drug regime. All three participants also reported improved quality of life. The study’s main goal, however, was to gauge safety. The viral carrier has a relatively established safety record, but high doses have been linked to severe immune reactions and even deaths . Delivering the therapy directly into brain tissue requires far smaller doses than when injected into the bloodstream and perhaps, counterintuitively, could be safer overall. Blood tests, brain scans, and other assessments find no major side effects. One patient experienced a temporary rise in liver enzymes, a sign of liver stress, but levels returned to normal without intervention. The team plans to expand the trial, but there are plenty of unsolved questions. All three men continued taking their existing antiseizure medications throughout the trial, making it difficult to isolate the treatment’s effects. For example, could clozapine have somehow synergized with those medications to reduce seizure counts? The study was also open-label, without a placebo control. And clozapine, when taken at high doses, carries risks of heart and other problems , though the doses given here were much lower than those used in psychiatric disorders. Whether chemogenetics can deliver lasting seizure relief in larger groups remains to be seen. But its debut in human medicine is a hopeful glimpse of what’s possible, not just for epilepsy, but potentially for addiction, mood disorders, and other neurological conditions involving unbalanced brain circuits too. “These findings offer initial proof of concept,” the team wrote. The post Novel Gene Therapy Nearly Erases ‘Drug Resistant’ Seizures appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Wind turbines are designed to last for 20–25 years. By that measure, turbines around the world are an elderly lot. In the US alone, 7,500 wind turbines are at least 20 years old . As these clean energy-generating behemoths approach the end of their lives , their green reputation gets tainted. That’s because their large blades end up in landfills. Made to withstand the elements, turbine blades are so durable that breaking them down to recycle them is also not easy. But researchers at Tsinghua University have found a straightforward way to breathe new life into wind turbine blades. Their method turns old blades into two valuable manufacturing materials that can improve the mechanical and thermal properties of new blades. This new approach cuts greenhouse gas emissions by 83–92% compared to present-day recycling technique. The results can be found in the journal Chem Circularity . Wind turbine blades are made of tiny glass fibers in a resin that is made of chains that are linked closely. The fibers are difficult to separate from the resin for recycling. Existing recycling methods require rely on breaking down the resin with heat or chemical solvents. Besides consuming a lot of energy and producing chemical waste, these processes weaken the fibers and results in low-value materials. The Tsinghua team ground blade waste into powder and mixed it with carbon black. Then they place the mixture between electrodes and blast it with short intense pulses of electricity, using a technique called Flash Joule Heating. Therein lies a massive opportunity to decarbonize the grid. At these blistering temperatures, carbon reacts with silica to form silicon carbide, which is a tough, heat-resistant compound. Carbon atoms also reorganize into a one atom-thick lattice with a honeycomb structure, called graphene. Graphene, a material whose discoverers garnered the Nobel Prize, is known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity. The process converted close to 60% of the mixture into a silicon carbide–graphene composite made up of 34% silicon carbide and 66% graphene. The researchers then added this composite to fresh epoxy resin for making new blades. Just 0.3% by weight of the additive made the new resin stiffer and stronger, which should increase lifetime of new blades. The researchers’ calculations also show that at commercial scale the new blade recycling approach could turn a profit of about $80 per ton of material because the recovered silicon carbide and graphene are valuable. Heat and chemical-based recycling methods, by comparison, cost $460 per ton and $1,800 per ton respectively, they say. “Many emerging waste streams, including aerospace composites, automotive lightweight structures, electronic encapsulants, and fiber-reinforced construction materials, share similar challenges,” the team writes in the paper. Their approach hints at a way to deal with those waste streams. The team is now working on ways to scale up their process. Source: Hao Bi et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Trust and Climate-Smart Agriculture Scaling Depend More on Neighbors Than Institutions, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes A study of 514 Central American farmers found that trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling are closely linked, with relationships with neighbors mattering more than trust in outside organizations. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling have long been treated as separate concerns, one social, one technical. New research published in Agricultural Systems directly challenges that separation, showing that farmer-to-farmer relationships shape whether climate innovations spread at all, regardless of how well-designed they are on paper. Researchers from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, the University of Copenhagen, and the Gates Foundation analyzed data from 514 smallholder farmers participating in Climate-Smart Villages, known locally as Territorios Sostenibles Adaptados al Clima, across Guatemala and Honduras. The study examined how different dimensions of social capital influence knowledge sharing about climate-smart practices, and what that process reveals about the earliest stages of responsible scaling. The findings reframe how funders and policymakers should evaluate trust and the scaling of climate-smart agriculture. Success is traditionally measured only after an innovation has already reached large numbers of adopters. This study instead focuses on an earlier moment: when farmers first share experiences, discuss new practices, raise questions, and learn from one another, long before adoption becomes visible at any meaningful scale. Trust among farmers emerged as the single most consistent factor enabling knowledge sharing. When farmers trust one another, they are much more likely to share experiences, discuss new practices, and learn from each other’s successes and failures. Close relationships among farmers further strengthen these learning networks, making it easier for knowledge and hands-on experience to circulate freely within a community rather than remaining isolated within individual households. Perhaps the study’s most striking finding for trust and scaling climate-smart agriculture is the role of mutual support. Researchers found that support between farmers becomes especially critical in communities where trust remains low. In these lower-trust environments, guidance, collaboration, and the exchange of practical experience help sustain knowledge flows that trust alone would otherwise fail to carry. Mutual support effectively functions as a backup mechanism, compensating for weaker social bonds that might otherwise block information sharing entirely. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling depend heavily on mutual support in low-trust communities, where researchers found that guidance and collaboration between farmers help sustain the flow of knowledge that institutional trust alone fails to provide. Photo by Frank Meriño on Pexels. By contrast, the research found that trust in formal organizations, whether government agencies, NGOs, or research institutions, carried notably less influence than trust built directly among farmers themselves. This distinction matters enormously for how development programs are typically designed, since many climate-smart agriculture initiatives invest heavily in institutional credibility and extension services while underinvesting in the peer networks that this study identifies as more decisive. Researchers also found a positive association between adopting climate-smart practices and knowledge sharing, reinforcing that these two processes reinforce each other rather than operating independently. A farmer observing a neighbor successfully implementing a drought-coping technique, discussing the results, adapting that practice to their own land’s specific conditions, and later sharing their experience with others exemplifies the kind of organic circulation of trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research seeks to capture and understand. These findings carry direct implications for how governments, development organizations, and innovation programs design their interventions. The evidence suggests development organizations need to place social dynamics at the center of scaling strategies rather than treating community relationships as secondary to technical training and resource distribution. Programs that invest in building trust and facilitating informal peer networks, rather than relying solely on top-down institutional messaging, appear better positioned to achieve the kind of local ownership that sustains results over time. Trust and climate-smart agriculture scaling research also supports what the study authors describe as a responsible scaling approach, one that anticipates and manages unintended consequences before they emerge rather than addressing problems only after widespread adoption has already occurred. Understanding how knowledge circulates among farmers before adoption becomes visible allows program designers to build strategies that are more inclusive, more context-sensitive, and more attuned to the specific social fabric of the communities they aim to serve. As agrifood systems worldwide face mounting pressure to accelerate climate adaptation, this research corrects purely technical approaches to scaling innovation. The impact of any climate-smart agricultural practice depends not only on its scientific merit, but equally on farmers’ capacity to share knowledge, learn collaboratively, and build the relationships of trust that let that knowledge travel organically through a community, often well before any formal program measures success. The post Trust and Climate-Smart Agriculture Scaling Depend More on Neighbors Than Institutions, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: This story was originally published by Grist . Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here . Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain. Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer. Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons . Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO2 washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy of Teresus Solutions Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place. Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on. In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps and compressors. Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one-third of what’s inside a full scuba tank . As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp. The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’ chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing. For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry. The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said. As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint. Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance? LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work. LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to remove sugars, salts and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS , raising questions about environmental trade-offs. Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.” Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously. The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag . CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium. Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend. The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question. Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance. items.descriptionOriginal: Garry oak trees, home for bluebirds nested in cavities, were tended by First Nations for millennia. Without their care, 95 percent of the Garry oak ecosystem was lost to agriculture, pesticides, and urban development. Their homes gone, bluebirds left, and were declared extinct on Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. “Garry oak trees are a great source of insects,” said Jacquie Taylor, coordinator for the Cowichan Bring Back the Bluebirds Project. “They have a real biodiversity of their own, things that live in the bark and on the trees.” Saving them would help save the bluebirds. Canadians and Americans worked together, along with a military base, a slew of permits, thousands of volunteer hours, private property owners, Cowichan Tribes, and lots and lots of tiny, wriggling mealworms to help the bluebirds return. “But most noticeable is the sound: a gentle musical chortling so cheerful and soothing that it immediately banishes all thought of the ills of the world.”

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Watershed Restoration in Ethiopia Reaches First Major Milestone Reading Time: 3 minutes Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone as 1,000 community members planted 152,333 seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds in the Tana Subbasin. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia reached a new milestone in July, with more than 1,000 community members planting over 150,000 tree seedlings across four degraded micro-watersheds . The effort marks ProTana’s first major field campaign, a five-year project led by the World Resources Institute and partners. Nearly half of the volunteers were women. ProTana focuses on the Tana Subbasin in Ethiopia’s Amhara Region, home to Lake Tana, the country’s largest lake and the source of the Blue Nile. The lake and its surrounding watersheds supply water for millions of people across the region. Decades of deforestation, overgrazing, and soil erosion have steadily degraded the land feeding into it. Lake Tana’s importance reaches well beyond Ethiopia’s borders. Water flowing out of the lake eventually joins the Blue Nile, which supplies a significant share of the water reaching Sudan and Egypt downstream. Keeping the watersheds that feed the lake healthy therefore affects water security across the wider Nile basin, not just the communities living closest to it. The World Resources Institute (WRI) is implementing the project alongside WaterAid Ethiopia and ORDA Ethiopia, focusing on three districts: North Mecha, Farta, and Dera. Selecting which specific watersheds to restore took months of consultation with local officials and community leaders. Criteria included erosion severity, the importance of water supply, and each community’s willingness to participate. The four selected micro-watersheds span more than 2,100 hectares combined. During July’s planting campaign, workers and volunteers put in over 152,000 seedlings, split between private agroforestry plots and communal or institutional land. Planting took place at the start of Ethiopia’s main rainy season to give seedlings the best chance of survival. Community turnout exceeded expectations, with more than 1,000 people taking part directly. Many children and young people also attended, watched the planting process, and learned why restoring the land matters for their future water security. Organizers see early engagement as key to building long-term support, since restoration work without community buy-in rarely survives past its first planting season. Watershed restoration in Ethiopia drew more than 1,000 community participants, with children and young people watching and learning alongside adults, as organizers bet that early engagement is the only way to build the long-term community buy-in that keeps restoration work alive past its first planting season. Photo by Khedir Dawed, courtesy of World Resources Institute . This campaign builds on an earlier three-year pilot in the Minzir 01 micro-watershed, part of the same broader area. That pilot showed measurable improvements in local water supply alongside benefits for nearby crop farming. ProTana now aims to apply those same lessons across a much larger area. Tree planting represents only the first phase of watershed restoration in Ethiopia under this project. Future work will include soil and water conservation measures such as terracing, check dams, and soil bunds. Regenerative agricultural practices are also planned to help households manage land more sustainably over the long term. A WRI program specialist working on the project described success as depending heavily on strong local leadership and coordination between partners. He noted that when communities see real benefits firsthand, they tend to stay far more committed to protecting restored land afterward, rather than treating conservation as an outside obligation imposed on them. According to the World Resources Institute, watershed restoration in Ethiopia fits into a broader strategy addressing water risk, climate resilience, and sustainable water governance across the country. The organization continues to monitor seedling survival through the rainy season to track how well the new plantings take hold. If ProTana’s larger rollout matches the results seen in its earlier pilot, this round of watershed restoration in Ethiopia could improve water availability and livelihoods for thousands of households in the Tana Subbasin. Much of that outcome will depend on how well new seedlings survive and how consistently local institutions keep up conservation work after the initial planting rush ends. For now, the scale of community turnout offers an early, encouraging sign that residents are ready to stay involved for the long haul. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Concentrations of PFOS and PFOA, the two most toxic forever chemicals , have fallen by 30 percent and 29 percent in England’s rivers over the past 10 years, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA). In freshwater fish , levels are down 49 percent. The agency attributes the decline to restrictions that removed both compounds from most products, which makes the data one of the clearer measures yet of what a chemical ban does to a river system over time. Two forever chemicals, two bans, one decade of data PFOS and PFOA PFAS, short for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were first developed in the U.S. in the 1930s. Manufacturers adopted them for their resistance to oil, water, and heat, and they ended up in nonstick pans, firefighting foam, and electrical components. The same chemical stability means they take a very long time to break down, which earned them the label forever chemicals. PFOS and PFOA were among the earliest compounds in the family. About 20 years ago, researchers began linking them to tissue damage in animals and to higher rates of certain serious illnesses in people, including testicular cancer . The UK all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020. Results from the latest Environment Agency figures The new data, published by the EA this month, covers 10 years of monitoring. Both chemicals declined by nearly a third in river water, while the near-halving in fish points to less of the compounds moving up the food chain. Dr. David Megson, a reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University, welcomed the trend. “It’s brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years,” he said. Lower concentrations, same total load Where forever chemicals go after a ban The EA report attaches a significant caveat to its own numbers. Because PFOS and PFOA break down so slowly, the total quantity in the environment has likely not changed much. Concentrations in rivers have dropped because the chemicals have been diluted and carried downstream into the sea. A ban stops new inputs, but it does not remove what is already circulating. Very few methods can destroy PFAS permanently. High-temperature incineration is one of them, and England currently has only two facilities suited to the job. Making polluters pay Megson sees the monitoring record as a starting point for accountability. “There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused,” he said. Regulating PFAS as a group 15,000 compounds, 200 in common use PFOS and PFOA are two of an estimated 15,000 PFAS, of which around 200 are in frequent use. The EA said that “uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS” and that its findings reinforce the case for regulating the chemicals as a class instead of one at a time. The chemicals industry has long resisted a group approach, arguing that evidence of toxicity for most other PFAS is limited or absent and that some have essential applications, including in life-saving medical equipment. Wider monitoring The agency now tests regularly for 60 additional PFAS to map contamination across England, and the government announced earlier this month that it will begin measuring forever chemicals in people’s bodies. Taken together with the river data, those programs will show whether the pattern seen with PFOS and PFOA holds for other compounds once restrictions arrive: a slow but steady fall in water and wildlife, with the legacy load still to be dealt with downstream. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM It’s 6 p.m. on a Friday, and the dinner you booked two weeks ago is in an hour. Back then it sounded like the perfect plan. But now your couch has never looked softer, your sweatpants feel like a hug, and your thumb is hovering over a message that starts with “So sorry, something came up…” Nothing came up, of course. You just don’t want to go anymore, and you can’t quite explain why. If that sounds familiar, you have plenty of company. According to the Survey Center on American Life , 55 percent of Gen Z adults say they feel relief when plans fall through. In the U.K., research from the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that 68 percent of people under 34 have bailed on plans, and one in 10 do it “very often.” There’s a name for that late-afternoon dread, and once you can name it, it gets a lot easier to put your shoes on anyway. What anticipatory anxiety feels like The doorway as a dividing line Mindy DeSeta , a licensed mental health counselor, calls it anticipatory anxiety. “It’s the stress we feel before something happens,” she says. Part of the pull comes from home itself, which is familiar and predictable in a way a crowded restaurant isn’t. “Walking through the doorway is the visual trigger that separates your safe space from the unknown,” DeSeta said. It’s the same jittery feeling you might have had before a school recital or a big presentation at work, just pointed at something that’s supposed to be fun. Why the dread rarely matches the night Think back to the last time you went out despite wanting to cancel. Chances are, an hour in, you were laughing at something and had forgotten all about the couch. DeSeta has seen that pattern again and again. “In most cases, the anticipation anxiety is often worse than the event itself. Don’t allow the jitters to deter you!” she said. What canceling plans costs your friends When everyone bails, everyone feels it Canceling feels harmless in the moment, and sometimes it’s the right call. But when it becomes a habit for a whole generation, someone is always on the other end of that text. Rachel Schleider, a 23-year-old social strategist said her birthday has become a source of stress for exactly this reason. “I literally dread making plans for my birthday every year because I know people are going to cancel the day before,” she said. She thinks the culture around flaking has swung too far. “We’ve kind of taken it too far and now people are way too comfortable bowing out,” Schleider said. How to manage anticipatory anxiety before a plan Name it, then don’t negotiate with it DeSeta’s first suggestion is to call the feeling what it is. Once you recognize the dread as anticipatory anxiety, you can remind yourself that the feeling isn’t an instruction. Feeling uneasy about going is a different thing from having a reason not to go. Breathe, and look at what the nerves are telling you A few slow, deep breaths can take the edge off the physical side of it, the tight chest and the restless hands. It also helps to flip the meaning of the nerves around. Feeling jittery about seeing someone usually means the plan matters to you, which is a reason to show up instead of a reason to stay home. Set an alarm and let the routine carry you DeSeta’s most practical trick happens before the dread has a chance to build: set an alarm for when you need to start getting ready, and when it goes off, get in the shower and get dressed without debating it. By the time your hair is dry, you’re most of the way out the door. None of this means you should drag yourself out when you’re sick or running on empty. Rest is a valid reason to cancel. But if the only thing standing between you and your friends is that familiar pre-plan heaviness, it might help to picture the walk home afterward, a little tired and full and glad you went, and let that version of the evening make the decision for you. There’s a name for that feeling first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers Reading Time: 4 minutes From Daily Rides to Pro Races, Cycling Comes In Many Forms. Here’s a Simple Guide to Each One What Do You Mean by Cycling? Everyday Riding for a Greener Life The cost of gas and vehicle repairs and maintenance has many people looking at cycling as an alternative way to get around, but what do you mean by cycling exactly? Depending on where you’re cycling and your purpose for doing the activity, there are different types of cycling available for you. Some people are just looking to get places on main streets, while others are more adventurous and want to explore with off-road cycling. There are many different types of cycling , so let’s take a closer look at what the best might be for you. The Best Bicycle for Beginners So you think you want to give cycling a try. But what is the best bicycle for beginners ? As we already talked about, it really depends on the type of cycling you’re wanting to get into. There are many different types of cycling, and your equipment needs to fit the type that you are doing. Anyone who bikes regularly knows that each has its own needs, so your equipment needs to match where and how you’re going to be cycling. Different Types of Cycling: Road, Track, Mountain and More So what are the different types of cycling? There are many, as the sport has few limits on how you decide to approach it. For getting places and more relaxing rides, there is road cycling. This occurs – as the name implies – on roads, so there isn’t much terrain to worry about. The bike for road cycling is more sleek and aerodynamic, allowing for smoother rides on the smoother terrain that is being used. This leads to track cycling, where speed is more of a concern. The cycle and the attire of the cyclist are made for less wind resistance and greater speeds. Mountain biking comes with less predictable terrain, so the cycle itself must have more of a suspension system and wider tires to help the cyclist deal with the different obstacles that come up. There is less of a need for being aerodynamic with the cycle and the attire, since this type of cycling is more focused on getting through off-road trails. Another of the types of cycling is gravel cycling, which is a bit of a cross between mountain biking and road cycling. As you might guess, this type is on gravel trails, which brings fewer obstacles and a bit more stability on trails than mountain biking. The type of bike for this is a cross between mountain biking and road cycling, with wider tires but less suspension. A growing form of cycling is e-biking, which can be applied to almost any form of cycling. This is not a motorcycle or moped, as the cyclist still has to be doing work. The motor and battery on an e-bike assist when needed to make for longer rides and easier times for cyclists when they face obstacles like a steep climb. There are also racing forms of cycling, whether on streets like the Tour de France or over ramps and jumps in BMX racing. Types of Bicycle Racing in the Olympics When it comes to racing, the top venue for cycling is the Olympics. There are five different disciplines that are held in the Summer Olympic Games. Road cycling is done on outdoor courses with a mass-start road race. Also on outdoor courses is mountain bike racing, with rougher natural terrain, steep climbs, and obstacles. One of the more popular types of bicycle racing at the Olympics is track cycling, which is held on a banked oval track using fixed-gear bicycles with no brakes. There are multiple different events within this form of cycling, including team pursuit and sprints. There are two types of BMX racing in the Olympics as well. BMX racing is held on dirt tracks with as many as eight cyclists running the course filled with jumps and banked turns at a time. There is also BMX freestyle, which is a judged competition as riders perform tricks in a one-minute run on a park course. Bicycle Racing Categories Every Fan Should Know One of the most popular bicycle racing categories , or sporting events, in the world is the Tour de France, which is a stage race over multiple days that tests a cyclist’s endurance and strategy. Cyclists have stages that they complete each day, with the Tour de France having 21 stages over three weeks. It has made stars out of past winners like Greg LeMond and Lance Armstrong, and is also a big betting event for fans. Speaking of betting, you can see BetUS Sportsbook odds to win the 2027 Tour de France. There is also a form of racing called criteriums, which are shorter races in both distance and time but are just as spectator- and betting-friendly. These are often on street courses like auto racing, with the cyclists going around a track and past spectators. You can also find road races that are held over street courses for longer distances. These can be held with a mass start (everyone all at once), or in individual time trials where cyclists start in staggered intervals. FAQs What are the different types of cycling? There are many different types of cycling, from road cycling, mountain biking, gravel cycling, BMX cycling, e-biking, and track cycling. Which type of cycle is best for racing? The type of cycle needed for racing depends on the type of racing being done. Track or road cycling is different from off-road or BMX racing. Each type of racing requires a different kind of bicycle. How is a gravel bike different from a mountain bike? A gravel bike is made to be a combination of a mountain bike and a road bike, so it has the look of a road bike but the features of a mountain bike as well. They have wider tires and a more relaxed frame to give more versatility than a straight mountain bike. The post Types of Cycling Explained for Eco Riders and Race Followers appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Energy Behind Online Casinos: Can Digital Gaming Run on Cleaner Power? Reading Time: 3 minutes Every spin, stream, and click runs on electricity somewhere. Here’s where that energy goes, and how cleaner power is changing the picture. Energy consumption of online gaming isn’t at the forefront of players’ minds when they log in and get ready for a playing session. It is on the mind of those who are behind the scenes and running these sites and platforms. How Much Energy Does Online Gaming Use? Online casino energy consumption is a huge factor. Every game on a screen sits on a server working away in a data center. That would be every game that is played; add in live streams and shows that are hosted, and other essentials to get the performance that is expected, and it turns into an electricity spending spree. The Carbon Footprint of Online Gaming The carbon footprint depends on where the electricity comes from. And it is definitely a source where online gaming businesses are trying to find ways to lower the costs of operation. The more streamlined a business, the better it can serve its customers … and its operations. Research shows gaming represents $5 billion per year in energy expenditures across the United States, with carbon-dioxide emissions equivalent to that of 85 million refrigerators or over 5 million cars. According to the International Energy Agency, data centers globally consumed approximately 460 terawatt-hours in 2022, accounting for nearly 2% of total electricity demand. That was almost five years ago. Imagine what the number is now as more and more people turn to online gaming for entertainment. Rising computing power, improved graphics quality, higher-resolution displays, and streaming delivery have rendered computer gaming an increasingly energy-intensive activity. Green data centers are a big piece of the equation in this business, as sites try to find ways to be more economical and prudent. Green Data Centers and the Shift to Cleaner Power There are options, for sure. An eco-friendly online casino operation understands that wind and solar are powering more of the internet. Green data centers rely on renewables, smarter cooling, and efficient servers. The cooler the center, the less energy is drained. Cooling methods for servers can account for 40% of the total energy consumption, hence the carbon footprint of online gaming. And, with the rising electricity demand worldwide … Small Changes That Make Gaming Greener Not every fix needs a power plant. Efficient software, lighter websites, and energy-saving devices can help the cause. Additionally, liquid cooling technology and smart temperature management systems can reduce energy usage dramatically, according to Uptime Institute research. What an Eco-Friendly Online Casino Looks Like Picture a platform built to be lean, fast, and efficient. Leading online gambling operators are increasingly adopting sustainable data centers and green data center practices, including: Implementation of energy-efficient servers and hardware, use of renewable energy sources for power, advanced heat recycling systems, AI-powered optimization of server loads, and geographic positioning in naturally cool climates. This all moves in the direction of sustainable online gaming, such as for those who play any of the casino games available at BetUS , for example. It’s good to know that modern casinos like BetUS Casino offer quick, digital payouts with less waste. The less waste, the less energy, and the greater the feasibility of the business. Heading in the direction of eco-friendly server infrastructure is needed for sustainable online gambling operations. FAQs Are online casinos greener than land-based casinos? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Reading Time: 2 minutes PET Cans vs Aluminium Cans: What Producers Should Know About Recyclability and Lightweighting Understanding Beverage Container Evolution The beverage packaging industry continually seeks materials that balance structural integrity, consumer appeal, and environmental responsibility. Producers must evaluate various packaging formats to meet shifting regulatory demands and sustainability targets. Two prominent contenders in modern production lines are the traditional metal cylinder and the transparent polymer vessel. Understanding their distinct characteristics regarding material recovery and mass reduction helps brand owners make informed decisions for their product portfolios. The Mechanics of Lightweighting Lightweighting remains a primary strategy for reducing transport emissions and material consumption. Aluminium packaging has historically achieved significant mass reduction through advanced wall-ironing techniques, resulting in thin, rigid walls that withstand internal pressure. On the other hand, the PET can offers unique advantages in mass optimization because polymer distribution can be precisely controlled during the stretch blow molding process. This allows manufacturers to tailor wall thickness to specific product requirements, whether packaging still water or carbonated beverages. Recycling Infrastructure and Material Recovery End-of-life processing heavily influences the overall sustainability footprint of any packaging format. Metal recycling systems are globally mature, allowing aluminium to be melted down repeatedly without losing its core mechanical properties. Polymer recovery has also advanced significantly, with dedicated sorting facilities capable of processing clear and colored containers efficiently. Both materials fit into circular economy models, though the specific infrastructure varies by geographic region. Key Production Considerations When selecting between these two packaging formats, producers must analyze several operational factors: Filling line compatibility and conversion costs for existing equipment Barrier properties required to protect product shelf life against oxygen and light Consumer perception of touch, transparency, and tactile experience Supply chain resilience and raw material price volatility Balancing Sustainability Goals Ultimately, the choice between metal and polymer containers depends on specific brand priorities and distribution models. While metal provides permanent recyclability, polymers offer design versatility and complete product visibility. By carefully assessing lightweighting potential and local recovery streams, producers can optimize their packaging strategy for long-term operational success. items.descriptionOriginal: When people coined the proverb that “mighty oaks from little acorns grow”, they certainly weren’t thinking of Lyme disease. But literal acorns—not poetic metaphors—turn out to play a surprisingly big role in the spread of this mighty tick-borne illness, according to a recent paper in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences . A surge in acorns one year can translate into a boom two years later in the population of ticks that transmit the disease to people. This discovery illustrates the ways in which a web of tiny, interconnected things—acorns, mice, microbes—can have big and unexpected consequences for people. It also shows that it can take decades of scientific research to decipher the head-scratching complexity of ecosystems. The results are “helping us to inform management of tick-borne disease risk,” said Shannon LaDeau, one of the paper’s authors and an ecologist with the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York State’s Hudson River Valley. LaDeau and colleague Richard Ostfeld oversee a Lyme-related research program at the institute that stretches back more than 30 years, just a few decades after the disease was first identified. Over that time, scientists have turned plots of New York forestland into an outdoor Lyme laboratory. They’ve assembled mountains of data tracking the ups and downs of a huge range of elements: temperature, rainfall, oak seedlings, mouse populations, tick numbers, infection rates, you name it. The results have repeatedly surprised scientists, defying expectations about the disease. It’s been known since the 1980s that the disease is caused by the bacteria Borrelia burgdorferi. The bite of an infected deer tick transmits the bacterium to people, causing flu-like symptoms that can escalate to chronic fatigue, memory loss, depression and even brain swelling and cardiac problems. More than 450,000 cases are reported in the U.S. each year, plus more than 200,000 in Europe. Despite the tick’s association with deer, the Cary Institute work didn’t bear out initial suspicions that more white-tailed deer translated into more dangers for people. The researchers found no correlation between deer numbers and the abundance of tick nymphs—the life stage when they most commonly transmit the disease to people. Nor did they find a link to seasonal temperature extremes. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , Lyme Disease: Prescribed fire Instead, the researchers uncovered evidence of a cascade of cause and effect between oak trees, white-footed mice and ticks. Acorns from red oak trees at the study sites are a primary food source for the mice. The year after a big acorn harvest, the mouse population boomed, the scientists found. The mice, in turn, are a prime feeding target for larval ticks which go on to become nymphs the following year. A big year for mice translated into a roughly 40% increase in abundance of tick nymphs the next year. All this thanks to a bumper crop in acorns two years earlier. While acorns aren’t abundant everywhere that the disease occurs, fluctuations in other crucial mouse food, such as seeds, could have the same effect, the scientists wrote. While it took years to tease apart these dynamics, researchers were still puzzled by other patterns. A surge in mice meant more ticks—and therefore a greater risk of people getting infected. But it didn’t translate into a higher percentage of the ticks themselves carrying the disease, the data showed. “It kept me up at night,” Ostfeld said of the result. “It meant that my understanding of how the system works was incomplete or wrong.” An apparent answer emerged when the researchers looked not just at the mouse population, but at a variety of small mammals. The long-term study plots were located in relatively intact forest that supported a range of other warm-blooded critters, such as skunks, squirrels and opossums. Many of these creatures are less prone to getting infected when a tick feeds on them, which also means they are less likely to spread the bacteria to other ticks. As a consequence, the percentage of infected ticks was driven not just by the number of mice but the population of a range of creatures. By contrast, in nearby places where forests had been broken into pieces by human intrusion , the diversity of small mammals was smaller. In those spots, where ticks had fewer options, higher mouse numbers did translate into more infected ticks. So in addition to small things like acorns, add two very big things that shape people’s risk of encountering Lyme disease: loss of habitat and of biodiversity. items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. Get smart Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans. Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. Will says: As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. Mapping roots In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. “I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” Becca says: On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable tree. On the other hand, I do like the idea of people detouring to see cool trees . What else we’re reading Minnesota announces ‘effective end’ to veteran homelessness, achieving decades-long goal — shared by Contributing Editor Michaela Haas from KSTP Free tool helps young men to take responsibility for sexual harm — shared by Contributing Editor Geetanjali Krishna from Positive News ‘Music is the most powerful way of connecting to what’s happening’: can this album change your mind about the climate crisis? — shared by Michaela Haas from the Guardian In other news… Turns out people love moss! Our Instagram video about how moss is taking over cities has really taken off. To learn more about all the cool things moss can do, read Michaela Haas’s great story. Αυτό που την έφερε πίσω ήταν μια φράση από έναν μέντορα: μείνετε πιστή σε αυτό που πραγματικά ακούτε από μέσα. Αυτή η γραμμή την ακολουθεί σε κάθε δωμάτιο από τότε. Μεγάλωσε σε ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: At fourteen, Shakhzoda Saidova slipped away from a conference table with the UN General Assembly and UNICEF in Tajikistan — too nervous, too convinced she didn't belong. What brought her back was a single sentence from a mentor: stay true to what you're actually hearing from inside. That line has followed her into every room since. She grew up in a country where her mother — who finished school with perfect marks and won a law scholarship — was forbidden by her husband's family from ever practicing as a lawyer. Watching that buried ambition became Shakhzoda's compass. Now studying in Romania, she is building SafeVoice: a disarmingly simple website listing real lawyers and crisis shelter numbers for women in Tajikistan facing domestic violence, because she knows what it costs a woman with three children and one free minute to find a page of dead links. She speaks five languages and is already being criticized for living in Europe at nineteen instead of being married. What's striking is the image of her mother, smiling serenely at those who disapprove — "Yes, I allowed that; yes, she's my daughter" — after accepting her daughter's diploma while the teenager boarded a flight towards a future she herself was never allowed to choose.
